description: ST elevation (STEMI) myocardial infarction of unspecified site
clinical_notes: Use I21.0–I21.2 for site-specific STEMI (anterior, inferior, lateral wall). Pair with I21.3 only when the occluded vessel territory is unspecified on discharge documentation. Requires additional code for coronary procedure (e.g., Z98.61 for coronary angioplasty status). Distinguish from NSTEMI (I21.4) using ECG criteria and troponin kinetics.
content: ICD-10 code I21.3 designates ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) of unspecified coronary artery territory, representing a complete occlusion of a coronary artery causing transmural myocardial necrosis. This is one of the highest-acuity cardiovascular emergency diagnoses in clinical practice and among the most consequential billing codes due to mandatory quality metrics. STEMI is defined by ST-segment elevation in two or more contiguous ECG leads with associated rising troponin I or T above the 99th percentile (greater than 0.04 ng/mL conventionally, or above sex-specific thresholds with high-sensitivity assays). Clinically, patients present with crushing chest pain often radiating to the left arm or jaw, diaphoresis, dyspnea, and nausea. The ACC/AHA 2022 guideline mandates first medical contact (FMC) to balloon time within 90 minutes for primary PCI — delays beyond this benchmark are tracked as a CMS quality measure. First-line management includes aspirin 325mg plus P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor preferred), unfractionated heparin, and emergent PCI. Fibrinolysis with alteplase is appropriate when PCI is unavailable within 120 minutes. Site-specific codes I21.0 (anterior wall), I21.1 (inferior wall), and I21.2 (lateral wall) are preferred when territory is documented; I21.3 is used when the infarct location is unspecified. Code I21.A1 designates STEMI due to coronary artery bypass graft occlusion. Related labs: troponin I (LAB-012), BNP/NT-proBNP (LAB-013), serum potassium (LAB-007) for electrolyte monitoring during reperfusion. Associated guideline: GUIDE-001 (ACC/AHA STEMI 2022). Disposition: Cardiac ICU. Condition reference: COND-001.

clinical_notes: Differentiate NSTEMI from unstable angina (I20.0): NSTEMI requires troponin elevation; unstable angina does not. Use I21.4 when troponin is elevated but ECG shows ST depression, T-wave changes, or no ST changes. Add Z87.39 for personal history of AMI if applicable. Risk stratify with GRACE score.
content: ICD-10 code I21.4 identifies Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI), representing partial coronary artery occlusion or severe stenosis causing subendocardial ischemia without transmural infarction. This code is one of the most frequently assigned acute cardiovascular emergency codes in hospital billing. The critical diagnostic distinction from STEMI (I21.3) is the absence of ST elevation on a 12-lead ECG, which may instead show ST depression, T-wave inversions, or be entirely normal — with the diagnosis resting on the presence of elevated troponin in the appropriate clinical context. Patients present with chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea, and fatigue. Atypical presentations are common in elderly patients, women, and those with diabetes, who may present with jaw pain, epigastric discomfort, or isolated dyspnea. Risk stratification using GRACE or TIMI score drives management intensity: high-risk features (elevated troponin, dynamic ECG changes, GRACE score above 140) warrant early invasive strategy with coronary angiography within 24 hours. Per ACC/AHA 2021 NSTEMI guidelines, first-line treatment includes aspirin 325mg loading followed by 81mg daily, P2Y12 inhibitor loading (ticagrelor 180mg preferred), anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin or enoxaparin, high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg), and beta-blocker for tachycardia or hypertension. Fibrinolysis is contraindicated in NSTEMI — it provides no benefit and increases harm compared to PCI. Serial troponin measurements at 0, 3, and 6 hours are essential for diagnosis and risk stratification. NSTEMI must be distinguished from unstable angina (I20.0), which shares clinical presentation but lacks troponin elevation. Related condition: COND-002. Guideline reference: GUIDE-002 (ACC/AHA 2021). Labs: troponin I (LAB-012), BNP (LAB-013).

clinical_notes: Specify HFrEF (I50.20–I50.23) vs HFpEF (I50.30–I50.33) when ejection fraction is documented. Acute decompensation adds I50.01 (acute) qualifier. Add codes for precipitating cause: hypertension (I10), AF (I48.x), ischemia (I21.x). CMS requires documentation of EF for risk adjustment. I50.9 used only when EF is not documented.
content: ICD-10 code I50.9 designates heart failure, unspecified, applied when heart failure is documented but left ventricular ejection fraction is not specified in the clinical record. This is among the highest-volume hospital admission diagnoses with significant CMS quality measure implications. Heart failure is classified by ejection fraction: HFrEF (reduced EF below 40%, codes I50.20–I50.23), HFmrEF (mildly reduced EF 40–49%, codes I50.810–I50.814), and HFpEF (preserved EF 50% or above, codes I50.30–I50.33). Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is characterized by acute worsening of signs and symptoms including dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, peripheral edema, rapid weight gain, jugular venous distension, and bilateral pulmonary crackles. The diagnosis is supported by BNP above 400 pg/mL or NT-proBNP above 900 pg/mL (LAB-013), pulmonary vascular congestion on chest X-ray, and reduced ejection fraction on echocardiogram. Per ACC/AHA/HFSA 2022 guidelines, the cornerstone of treatment is IV loop diuretic therapy with furosemide (2.5 times the home oral dose IV), targeting urine output of 3-5 liters in the first 24 hours. Sodium restriction below 2 grams per day and fluid restriction below 2 liters per day are essential. Guideline-directed medical therapy (ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) should be continued unless hemodynamic instability requires temporary withholding. Monitor serum potassium (LAB-007) and creatinine (LAB-008) every 8-12 hours during aggressive diuresis. Common precipitants include medication non-adherence, dietary sodium indiscretion, new-onset AF, ACS, and uncontrolled hypertension. Related condition: COND-003. Guideline: GUIDE-003. Disposition: Hospital admission; ICU if hemodynamically unstable.

clinical_notes: Classify AF as paroxysmal (I48.0), persistent (I48.11), long-standing persistent (I48.19), or chronic (I48.20) when documented. I48.91 applies when type is not specified. CHA2DS2-VASc score must be documented for anticoagulation decision-making. Always check TSH to exclude thyrotoxicosis as an AF trigger.
content: ICD-10 code I48.91 designates unspecified atrial fibrillation, the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia worldwide. AF is characterized by chaotic, disorganized atrial electrical activity causing loss of coordinated atrial contraction and an irregularly irregular ventricular response. More specific codes should be used when documented: paroxysmal AF (I48.0, terminates spontaneously within 7 days), persistent AF (I48.11, requires cardioversion), long-standing persistent (I48.19, lasting more than 12 months), and chronic or permanent AF (I48.20). Patients present with palpitations, irregular heartbeat, dizziness, fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise intolerance. The ECG hallmark is an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves replaced by a fibrillatory baseline. Management requires addressing two key pillars: rate control and stroke prevention. Rate control targets heart rate below 110 bpm using beta-blockers (metoprolol) or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem), with diltiazem avoided in HFrEF due to negative inotropy. Anticoagulation is guided by CHA2DS2-VASc score: score of 2 or more in men and 3 or more in women warrants oral anticoagulation, preferably with direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban or rivaroxaban) over warfarin for non-valvular AF. Cardioversion should be preceded by 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or TEE to exclude left atrial thrombus if AF duration exceeds 48 hours. Always evaluate thyroid function with TSH (LAB-018) as hyperthyroidism triggers AF. Electrolytes, particularly potassium (LAB-007), must be optimized before cardioversion. BNP (LAB-013) may be elevated from associated tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy. Bleeding risk is formally assessed using HAS-BLED score before anticoagulation initiation. Related condition: COND-004. Guideline: GUIDE-004 (ACC/AHA/HRS 2023). Disposition: ED or monitored floor for new-onset or rapid ventricular rate.

clinical_notes: I16.1 requires documented end-organ damage (hypertensive encephalopathy, AKI, ADHF, aortic dissection, acute MI, hypertensive retinopathy). Distinguish from I16.0 (hypertensive urgency: BP >180/120 without organ damage). Always add codes for the specific end-organ affected: N17.9 for AKI, I50.9 for heart failure, I63.9 for stroke.
content: ICD-10 code I16.1 designates hypertensive emergency, defined as severe blood pressure elevation (generally above 180/120 mmHg) with acute end-organ damage, distinguishing it critically from hypertensive urgency (I16.0), which lacks organ damage and is managed differently. End-organ manifestations requiring the I16.1 designation include hypertensive encephalopathy (altered mental status, headache, papilledema), acute kidney injury (rising creatinine, LAB-008), acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema, hypertensive retinopathy with papilledema, aortic dissection, STEMI/NSTEMI (elevated troponin, LAB-012), and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Always assign additional codes for the specific end-organ affected alongside I16.1. Patients present with severe headache, visual disturbances, chest pain, dyspnea, altered mental status, nausea, vomiting, and in severe cases seizures. Management requires ICU admission with continuous arterial blood pressure monitoring and IV antihypertensive therapy. The critical principle is controlled reduction: reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 10-20% in the first hour and no more than 25% in the first 24 hours — overly aggressive reduction causes ischemic stroke, MI, or acute tubular necrosis. Preferred IV agents include nicardipine infusion (5-15 mg/hr) for most cases, labetalol boluses or infusion for aortic dissection or perioperative hypertension, esmolol infusion for aortic dissection (precise titration), and sodium nitroprusside for refractory cases with caution for cyanide toxicity. IV hydralazine is used in hypertension of pregnancy. Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated — it causes unpredictable dangerous BP drops. In cocaine-induced crisis, beta-blockers alone are contraindicated (unopposed alpha stimulation). Related condition: COND-005. Guideline: GUIDE-014. Disposition: ICU mandatory.

clinical_notes: Use organism-specific codes when identified: J13 (pneumococcal), J14 (H. influenzae), J15.x (bacterial, various organisms), J16.x (other), J12.x (viral). J18.9 is appropriate when the causative organism is not identified. Add U07.1 for COVID-19 pneumonia if applicable. Always document PSI or CURB-65 score for site-of-care decisions.
content: ICD-10 code J18.9 designates pneumonia with unspecified causative organism, the default code when the pathogen is not identified microbiologically. Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is one of the most common causes of inpatient admission and hospitalization-related mortality, with severity determining site of care and antibiotic choice. Patients present with productive cough with purulent sputum, fever, chills, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, fatigue, and malaise. Physical examination reveals crackles or bronchial breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and increased tactile fremitus over the consolidation. Chest X-ray or CT shows lobar consolidation or infiltrate. Laboratory findings include leukocytosis on WBC count (LAB-004), elevated procalcitonin above 0.25 ng/mL suggesting bacterial etiology (LAB-020), and elevated CRP (LAB-023). Blood cultures are positive in 10-20% of bacteremic cases. Per IDSA/ATS 2019 guidelines, site of care is determined by PSI score or CURB-65 (confusion, BUN >19, respiratory rate ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65). Outpatient low-risk treatment: amoxicillin 1g TID for 5 days or doxycycline 100mg BID. Inpatient non-ICU: ceftriaxone 1g IV daily plus azithromycin 500mg IV. ICU or severe CAP: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin plus vancomycin or linezolid if MRSA risk factors exist. Procalcitonin-guided therapy allows safe early antibiotic discontinuation when values fall below 0.25 ng/mL. Aspiration pneumonia requires anaerobic coverage. Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigens should be obtained in ICU-level CAP. Use organism-specific codes (J13, J14, J15.x) when pathogen is documented. Related condition: COND-006. Guideline: GUIDE-006 (IDSA/ATS 2019).

description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with (acute) exacerbation
clinical_notes: J44.1 is the exacerbation code; use J44.0 for COPD with acute lower respiratory infection and J44.9 for unspecified COPD without exacerbation. Document GOLD classification (GOLD I–IV based on FEV1) and GOLD group (A, B, E based on symptoms and exacerbation history). Add codes for respiratory failure (J96.x) if present. Always document smoking status.
content: ICD-10 code J44.1 designates chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with acute exacerbation, representing acute worsening of COPD symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variation requiring a change in therapy. Acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) is defined by the Anthonisen criteria: increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence — with all three present constituting a Type 1 exacerbation requiring antibiotic therapy. AECOPD is one of the leading causes of emergency department visits, hospitalization, and loss of lung function over time. Physical examination reveals tachypnea, use of accessory respiratory muscles, prolonged expiratory phase, diffuse wheezing, decreased breath sounds, and in severe cases paradoxical abdominal breathing. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms; arterial blood gas (LAB-021) demonstrates hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35, pCO2 above 45 mmHg) in moderate-to-severe exacerbations. WBC count (LAB-004) may show leukocytosis if bacterial infection triggers the exacerbation; procalcitonin (LAB-020) helps guide antibiotic use. First-line treatment: nebulized short-acting bronchodilators (albuterol plus ipratropium), systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 40mg daily for 5 days — longer courses provide no additional benefit), antibiotics if sputum is purulent (azithromycin, doxycycline, or amoxicillin-clavulanate), supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 88-92% (avoid hyperoxia — suppresses hypoxic drive), and non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP for hypercapnic respiratory failure with pH below 7.35. Intubation is reserved for patients failing NIV. GOLD 2024 guidelines use the GOLD ABCD group classification to guide stable management. Related condition: COND-007. Guideline: GUIDE-018.

clinical_notes: Asthma codes require documentation of severity (intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, severe persistent) and whether an acute exacerbation is present. J45.51 = severe persistent with exacerbation. Use J45.901 for unspecified asthma with acute exacerbation. Prior intubation history is the strongest predictor of fatal asthma — document prominently. Status asthmaticus: J45.x1 codes.
content: ICD-10 code J45.51 designates severe persistent asthma with acute exacerbation, representing the highest-acuity asthma category requiring aggressive emergency management. Severe persistent asthma is characterized by continuous daytime symptoms, frequent nighttime awakenings, FEV1 below 60% predicted, and multiple emergency visits or hospitalizations. An acute exacerbation superimposed on severe persistent asthma represents a potentially life-threatening event. Clinically, patients present with severe dyspnea, inability to speak in full sentences, diffuse bilateral wheezing, tachypnea above 25 breaths per minute, tachycardia, oxygen saturation below 90%, and marked use of accessory muscles. Critical warning signs include a silent chest (cessation of wheezing from critically reduced airflow), pulsus paradoxus above 25 mmHg, and rising or normalizing pCO2 on ABG (LAB-021) — indicating respiratory muscle fatigue and impending respiratory arrest. Early ABG typically shows respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation; a shift to normal or elevated pCO2 is immediately life-threatening. Peak expiratory flow below 50% predicted or below 200 L/min indicates severe obstruction. Magnesium sulfate levels (LAB-025) are relevant as IV magnesium sulfate 2g over 20 minutes is a key adjunct in severe cases. First-line treatment: continuous albuterol nebulization, ipratropium nebulization, IV methylprednisolone 125mg (or oral prednisone 60mg if tolerated), IV magnesium sulfate 2g for severe/refractory cases, and supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 above 93%. Intubation and mechanical ventilation require permissive hypercapnia strategy (allow CO2 rise to prevent barotrauma from aggressive ventilation in obstructed airways). Prior intubation for asthma is the single strongest predictor of fatal exacerbation and must be documented. Related condition: COND-008.

description: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
clinical_notes: Code I26.09 designates massive PE with acute cor pulmonale (hemodynamic instability). I26.99 applies when hemodynamic instability is absent. Always document Wells or Geneva score, D-dimer result, and CT-PA findings. Add Z87.39 for personal history of VTE. DVT coding (I82.4x) should be assigned in addition when concurrent DVT is confirmed.
content: ICD-10 code I26.99 designates other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale, representing the most common PE coding scenario — hemodynamically stable PE confirmed by CT pulmonary angiography. Pulmonary embolism occurs when thrombus (usually from deep leg veins) occludes the pulmonary arterial system, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoxemia, and in severe cases right ventricular failure. Clinically, patients present with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis, and unilateral calf swelling if concurrent DVT is present. Massive PE (code I26.09) presents with hemodynamic instability — hypotension (systolic BP below 90 mmHg or MAP below 65) or cardiac arrest. Submassive PE represents the intermediate-risk category with preserved hemodynamics but evidence of right ventricular dysfunction. Diagnosis requires risk stratification using the Wells or Geneva PE score: low-probability patients receive D-dimer (LAB-014) first; a negative D-dimer below 500 ng/mL safely excludes PE. High probability patients proceed directly to CT pulmonary angiography. Additional markers include elevated troponin (LAB-012) indicating RV strain and elevated BNP (LAB-013) indicating RV dysfunction — both are prognostic. Hypoxemia on ABG (LAB-021) with respiratory alkalosis is typical. PESI or sPESI score guides prognostication and disposition. Per ESC/AHA 2023 guidelines, stable PE is treated with DOACs: rivaroxaban (15mg BID for 21 days then 20mg daily) or apixaban (10mg BID for 7 days then 5mg BID). Massive PE receives systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100mg over 2 hours plus UFH. Minimum anticoagulation duration is 3 months for provoked PE; indefinite for unprovoked. Related condition: COND-009. Guideline: GUIDE-009.

clinical_notes: Use complication-specific codes when applicable: E11.21 (nephropathy), E11.311 (mild NPDR), E11.40 (diabetic neuropathy), E11.51 (peripheral angiopathy). E11.9 applies only when no complications are documented. Always assign separate codes for cardiovascular comorbidities (hypertension I10, hyperlipidemia E78.5). HbA1c and eGFR should be documented for risk adjustment.
content: ICD-10 code E11.9 designates type 2 diabetes mellitus without complications, the most prevalent metabolic disorder globally and one of the highest-volume outpatient diagnoses. Type 2 DM is characterized by progressive insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency leading to chronic hyperglycemia. E11.9 is used only when no diabetes-related complications are documented; when complications exist, specific codes such as E11.21 for diabetic nephropathy, E11.311 for non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, E11.40 for diabetic neuropathy, or E11.51 for diabetic peripheral angiopathy should replace it. Diagnosis requires fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or above (LAB-010), HbA1c of 6.5% or above (LAB-011), or random glucose of 200 mg/dL or above with symptoms on two separate occasions. Per ADA 2024 guidelines, management starts with metformin 500mg BID titrated to 2000mg daily (if eGFR ≥30, LAB-008) combined with lifestyle intervention. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) are added regardless of HbA1c in patients with established ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD. Target HbA1c is below 7% for most adults. Comprehensive monitoring includes HbA1c every 3 months until stable, annual eGFR, annual urine albumin-creatinine ratio, annual lipid panel, annual foot exam, and annual or biennial dilated retinal exam. SGLT2 inhibitors must be held 3-4 days before surgery or prolonged fasting (euglycemic DKA risk). Annual vitamin B12 monitoring is required in patients on metformin for more than 4 years. Related condition: COND-010. Guideline: GUIDE-007 (ADA 2024). Disposition: Outpatient with structured follow-up every 3 months.

description: Other specified diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
clinical_notes: E10.10 = type 1 DM with DKA without coma; E11.10 = type 2 DM with DKA without coma; E13.10 = other specified DM with DKA. With coma: E10.11, E11.11, E13.11 respectively. Always assign additional code for the precipitant (sepsis, pneumonia, etc.). Anion gap must be documented — DKA endpoint is anion gap closure, not glucose normalization.
content: ICD-10 code E13.10 designates other specified diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma, one of the three main DKA codes alongside E10.10 (type 1 DM) and E11.10 (type 2 DM). DKA is a life-threatening endocrine emergency defined by the triad of hyperglycemia (glucose above 250 mg/dL, LAB-010), metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.3, bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L on ABG, LAB-021), and ketonemia. Patients present with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations (deep rapid breathing compensating for metabolic acidosis), fruity acetone breath odor, polyuria, polydipsia, and altered mental status ranging from confusion to coma. Serum potassium (LAB-007) is critically important: initial potassium may be falsely normal or elevated (acidosis shifts K+ extracellularly) despite total body depletion from vomiting and polyuria. Starting insulin before confirming potassium above 3.5 mEq/L risks fatal hypokalemia. Serum sodium (LAB-006) requires correction for hyperglycemia: add 1.6 mEq/L to measured sodium for each 100 mg/dL glucose above 100. Per ADA/Endocrine Society 2022 guidelines, treatment follows a strict sequence: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (normal saline 1-1.5 L/hr for 1-2 hours, then transition to 0.45% NS), potassium replacement before insulin initiation, insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr, dextrose added to IV fluids when glucose falls below 200 mg/dL (to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin to close the anion gap), bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9. The treatment endpoint is anion gap closure — not glucose normalization. Transition to subcutaneous insulin when anion gap closes, pH above 7.3, bicarbonate above 18, and patient tolerates oral intake. Related condition: COND-011. Guideline: GUIDE-008 (ADA 2022).

clinical_notes: Specify type when known: E06.3 (Hashimoto thyroiditis), E03.0 (congenital), E89.0 (post-procedural/post-thyroidectomy). E03.9 for unspecified. Myxedema coma: E03.5 with coma. Subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH, normal T4): E02. Always document TSH level and whether anti-TPO antibodies were tested.
content: ICD-10 code E03.9 designates hypothyroidism, unspecified, representing insufficient production of thyroid hormone by the thyroid gland, leading to generalized metabolic slowing. It is one of the most common endocrine disorders, affecting approximately 5% of the population with a strong female predominance. The most common cause is Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune, code E06.3), characterized by positive anti-TPO antibodies and lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid. Other causes include post-thyroidectomy (E89.0), post-radioactive iodine ablation, iodine deficiency, and medications such as amiodarone and lithium. Patients present insidiously with fatigue, weight gain despite normal appetite, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair thinning and loss, bradycardia, cognitive slowing, depression, menstrual irregularities (menorrhagia), myalgias, and periorbital edema. Physical examination may reveal a goiter, delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes, and non-pitting edema of extremities. Diagnosis is based on elevated TSH above 4.5 mIU/L with low free T4 below 0.8 ng/dL (LAB-018), confirming primary hypothyroidism. Subclinical hypothyroidism (code E02) shows elevated TSH with normal free T4 and may not require treatment in all patients. MCV (LAB-002) may be elevated from concurrent macrocytic anemia. Associated laboratory findings include hyperlipidemia (elevated LDL), macrocytic or normocytic anemia, hyponatremia, and elevated CK. First-line treatment is levothyroxine at approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day, taken on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast. In elderly patients or those with cardiac disease, initiate at 12.5-25 mcg/day and titrate slowly to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmias. TSH is rechecked 6-8 weeks after dose adjustments. Myxedema coma (E03.5) is a life-threatening hypothyroid emergency requiring IV levothyroxine and hydrocortisone. Related condition: COND-012.

description: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter without thyrotoxic crisis or storm
clinical_notes: Graves disease (E05.00 without crisis, E05.01 with crisis/thyroid storm). Toxic multinodular goiter: E05.20. Toxic adenoma: E05.10. Thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45) uses E05.01 and is a medical emergency. Always document TSI antibody results for Graves-specific coding. Add codes for complications: AF (I48.x), heart failure (I50.x).
content: ICD-10 code E05.00 designates thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter (Graves disease) without thyrotoxic crisis, representing autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) that bind and activate the TSH receptor, resulting in excessive and unregulated thyroid hormone production. Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in iodine-sufficient countries. Patients present with unintentional weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, excessive sweating, palpitations, sinus tachycardia or AF (I48.x), fine tremor, anxiety, irritability, diarrhea, insomnia, and proximal muscle weakness. Graves-specific features include exophthalmos (proptosis from orbital inflammation), pretibial myxedema (non-pitting shin plaques), and thyroid acropachy. Diagnosis requires markedly suppressed TSH below 0.1 mIU/L with elevated free T4 and/or free T3 (LAB-018), positive TSI antibodies specific for Graves disease, and diffusely elevated radioactive iodine uptake distinguishing Graves from thyroiditis. Treatment options include antithyroid drugs (methimazole 10-30mg daily as first choice; PTU 100-200mg TID in first trimester pregnancy due to methimazole teratogenicity), beta-blockers (propranolol 20-40mg TID) for symptomatic relief while awaiting euthyroid state, radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation, or thyroidectomy for large goiters or treatment failure. Thyroid storm (E05.01) is a life-threatening emergency triggered by physiological stress, diagnosed by Burch-Wartofsky score of 45 or above, requiring IV propylthiouracil or methimazole, IV potassium iodide (after antithyroid drugs), propranolol, hydrocortisone, and ICU-level care. Related condition: COND-013.

clinical_notes: N17.9 is unspecified AKI. Specify etiology when documented: N17.0 (ATN), N17.1 (acute cortical necrosis), N17.2 (acute medullary necrosis). Always assign additional codes for the underlying cause: N00.9 (acute nephritic syndrome/GN), L40.x (prerenal from burns), etc. KDIGO staging (1, 2, 3) should be documented for appropriate care intensity and risk adjustment.
content: ICD-10 code N17.9 designates acute kidney failure, unspecified, representing a rapid decline in glomerular filtration rate occurring over hours to days. AKI is defined by the KDIGO criteria: rise in serum creatinine (LAB-008) by 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours, or 1.5 times or more above baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6 or more consecutive hours. AKI is classified by etiology as prerenal (60-70%, from decreased renal perfusion: dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, hemorrhage, characterized by BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1 and FeNa below 1%), intrinsic renal (25-30%, from direct parenchymal injury: acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, characterized by muddy brown casts, FeNa above 2%), or postrenal (5-10%, from urinary obstruction: hydronephrosis on ultrasound). BUN (LAB-009) and serum potassium (LAB-007) are critical monitoring parameters — hyperkalemia is the most immediately life-threatening complication. Per KDIGO 2022 guidelines, management centers on identifying and treating the underlying cause, aggressive volume resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's or normal saline for prerenal AKI, immediate discontinuation of all nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACE inhibitors/ARBs in established AKI), and bladder outlet decompression for postrenal obstruction. Indications for emergent renal replacement therapy: refractory hyperkalemia above 6.5 mEq/L, severe metabolic acidosis with pH below 7.1, BUN above 100 mg/dL, uremic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy), or refractory volume overload. AKI Stage 2-3 warrants nephrology consultation. Related condition: COND-014. Guideline: GUIDE-011. Disposition: ICU for Stage 3; step-down for Stage 1-2.

clinical_notes: R65.20 = severe sepsis without septic shock. R65.21 = severe sepsis WITH septic shock (requires vasopressors). Always code the underlying infection first (e.g., J18.9 for pneumonia, N39.0 for UTI, A41.9 for septicemia) before R65.20/21. Organ dysfunction codes must be added: N17.9 (AKI), J96.x (respiratory failure), K72.x (liver failure). Sepsis documentation must explicitly state organ dysfunction.
content: ICD-10 code R65.20 designates severe sepsis without septic shock, representing life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Sepsis is coded as a combination code: the underlying infection source must be sequenced first (pneumonia, urinary tract infection, bacteremia, wound infection) followed by R65.20 for severe sepsis or R65.21 for septic shock. Septic shock (R65.21) specifically requires both vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP above 65 mmHg and serum lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation — this coding distinction carries significant reimbursement and quality implications. Diagnosis uses the SOFA score (increase of 2 or more points indicating organ dysfunction) and qSOFA (altered mentation, SBP ≤100, respiratory rate ≥22, with 2 or more suggesting sepsis risk). Critical laboratory markers include serum lactate (LAB-019) above 2 mmol/L indicating tissue hypoperfusion (above 4 mmol/L confers high mortality risk), elevated WBC count with left shift (LAB-004), elevated procalcitonin (LAB-020) supporting bacterial etiology, and rising creatinine indicating renal dysfunction. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle mandates: blood cultures before antibiotics (2 sets within 45 minutes), broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition (vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem), 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid for MAP below 65 or lactate above 4, norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor if fluid-refractory, and lactate remeasurement. Every hour of antibiotic delay increases mortality approximately 7%. Source control (abscess drainage, infected catheter removal, infected device explantation) is essential. De-escalate antibiotics at 48-72 hours based on culture results. Related condition: COND-017. Guideline: GUIDE-005. Disposition: ICU.

clinical_notes: Always investigate the underlying cause: D50.0 (secondary to blood loss, chronic), D50.1 (sideropenic dysphagia). In men and postmenopausal women, GI source must be excluded by endoscopy before attributing to dietary deficiency. Add code for the cause of iron deficiency: menorrhagia (N92.x), GI bleeding (K92.x), malabsorption (K90.x). Ferritin below 30 ng/mL is the diagnostic threshold.
content: ICD-10 code D50.9 designates iron deficiency anemia, unspecified, the most common cause of anemia worldwide, resulting from insufficient iron stores to support adequate hemoglobin synthesis. Iron deficiency anemia is a microcytic hypochromic anemia characterized by low hemoglobin (LAB-001), low MCV below 80 fL (LAB-002), and low ferritin below 30 ng/mL (LAB-003) — with ferritin being the most sensitive and specific single test for iron deficiency. Additional findings include low serum iron, elevated TIBC above 400 ug/dL, transferrin saturation below 20%, low reticulocyte count, and hypochromic microcytic red cells with pencil cells on peripheral smear. Patients present with fatigue, pallor, dyspnea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, pica (craving non-food substances like ice, clay, or dirt — called pagophagia when ice specifically), restless legs syndrome, brittle nails (koilonychia), angular cheilitis, and glossitis. Identifying and treating the underlying cause is as important as replacing iron stores: in premenopausal women, menstrual blood loss (D50.0) is most common; in men and postmenopausal women, gastrointestinal blood loss must be excluded by upper and lower endoscopy to rule out peptic ulcer disease, colon polyps, or colorectal malignancy. Celiac disease (K90.0) is an important cause of refractory iron deficiency anemia due to malabsorption. First-line treatment is oral ferrous sulfate 325mg (providing 65mg elemental iron) three times daily on an empty stomach with vitamin C to enhance absorption. IV iron formulations (ferric carboxymaltose, iron sucrose) are indicated for oral iron intolerance, malabsorption, or need for rapid repletion. Red cell transfusion is reserved for hemoglobin below 7 g/dL or symptomatic severe anemia. Related condition: COND-020.

description: Acute embolism and thrombosis of unspecified deep veins of lower extremity
clinical_notes: Specify location when known: I82.401 (right femoral), I82.402 (left femoral), I82.411 (right popliteal), I82.421 (right tibial). Distal (calf) DVT: I82.4y1/2. Add code for provoked vs unprovoked distinction in documentation — affects anticoagulation duration decision. Assign concurrent PE code (I26.x) if applicable. VTE prophylaxis status should be documented.
content: ICD-10 code I82.40 designates acute embolism and thrombosis of unspecified deep veins of the lower extremity, representing the formation of a blood clot in a deep vein (most commonly femoral, popliteal, or tibial veins) with significant risk of detachment and embolization to the pulmonary arteries causing pulmonary embolism. DVT and PE together constitute venous thromboembolism (VTE). Clinically, DVT presents with unilateral leg swelling (the most reliable sign), calf pain and tenderness, warmth, erythema, and pitting edema. Diagnosis follows a structured pathway: calculate the Wells DVT score (high pre-test probability goes directly to compression ultrasonography; low probability gets D-dimer testing with LAB-014). A negative D-dimer below 500 ng/mL effectively excludes DVT in low-probability patients. Compression ultrasonography is the gold standard, showing non-compressibility of the affected vein. Baseline coagulation studies (LAB-015) are obtained before initiating anticoagulation. First-line treatment is direct oral anticoagulation: rivaroxaban (15mg BID for 21 days then 20mg daily) or apixaban (10mg BID for 7 days then 5mg BID), which are preferred over traditional LMWH-to-warfarin bridging for convenience and safety. Anticoagulation duration: 3 months for provoked DVT with transient risk factor; indefinitely for unprovoked, cancer-associated, or recurrent DVT. IVC filter is reserved only for patients with absolute contraindications to anticoagulation. Thrombophilia workup (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome) is indicated for unprovoked DVT in patients under 50. Annual bleeding risk reassessment is required for patients on extended anticoagulation. Related condition: COND-021. Guideline: GUIDE-009.

clinical_notes: F33.0 = recurrent mild MDD; F33.1 = moderate; F33.2 = severe without psychotic features; F33.3 = severe with psychosis; F32.x codes for single episode. Always screen for bipolar disorder (F31.x) before starting antidepressants. Document PHQ-9 score for severity. Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale required at every visit. F33.9 for unspecified MDD.
content: ICD-10 code F33.0 designates major depressive disorder, recurrent, mild, representing a common but serious psychiatric condition requiring systematic pharmacological and psychotherapeutic management. MDD requires at least 5 of 9 DSM-5 criteria present nearly every day for 2 or more weeks: depressed mood, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia — one of these two must be present), significant weight change or appetite disturbance, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue or loss of energy, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, diminished concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation. The PHQ-9 is the validated severity tool: score 5-9 indicates mild depression (F33.0), 10-14 moderate (F33.1), 15-19 moderately severe (F33.2), and 20-27 severe (F33.2). Rule out medical causes: TSH for hypothyroidism (LAB-018), CBC for anemia (LAB-001), vitamin B12 deficiency, substance-induced mood disorder, and bipolar disorder (F31.x) — antidepressant monotherapy in undiagnosed bipolar disorder can precipitate manic switch. Per APA 2023 guidelines, first-line treatment is combination pharmacotherapy plus psychotherapy: SSRI (sertraline 50-200mg daily or escitalopram 10-20mg daily) plus cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Allow 4-6 weeks for adequate response assessment before switching. Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale is mandatory at every visit; SSRIs carry FDA Black Box Warning for increased suicidality in patients under 25 requiring weekly monitoring for the first 4 weeks. MAOIs are contraindicated within 14 days of SSRIs (potentially fatal serotonin syndrome). Hospitalize if active suicidal ideation with plan, psychotic features, or inability to care for self. Related condition: COND-022. Guideline: GUIDE-015.

description: Acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection, unspecified
clinical_notes: Specify etiology: K85.0x (idiopathic), K85.1x (biliary/gallstone), K85.2x (alcohol), K85.3x (drug-induced), K85.8x (other). With necrosis: K85.x2 (without infection) or K85.x3 (infected). Ranson criteria and BISAP score should be documented for severity staging. ALT >150 U/L strongly suggests biliary etiology.
content: ICD-10 code K85.9 designates acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection, unspecified etiology — representing acute inflammation of the pancreas with autodigestion by activated pancreatic enzymes. Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed by 2 of 3 criteria: characteristic epigastric pain radiating straight to the back worse after eating, serum lipase elevated 3 or more times the upper limit of normal (above 180 U/L, LAB-016), and characteristic findings on CT imaging (pancreatic edema, peripancreatic fluid collections). ALT elevation above 150 U/L (LAB-017) strongly suggests biliary/gallstone etiology. Serum calcium (LAB-024) may be critically low in severe pancreatitis from saponification. BUN (LAB-009) above 25 mg/dL on admission is a BISAP adverse criterion and predictor of mortality. Severity is assessed using BISAP score (BUN, impaired mental status, SIRS criteria, age above 60, pleural effusion — score 3 or above indicates severe pancreatitis) or Ranson criteria (5 or more = severe). Per AGA/ACG 2022 guidelines, key management steps include aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's at 250-500 mL/hr for 12-24 hours (LR superior to normal saline — reduces systemic inflammation), goal-directed resuscitation targeting urine output 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr and HR below 120, analgesia with IV hydromorphone or fentanyl, and early oral feeding as tolerated (enteral nutrition preferred over TPN if oral intake impossible beyond 72 hours). Gallstone pancreatitis requires ultrasound within 24 hours and cholecystectomy during the same admission for mild disease. ERCP within 24 hours if concurrent cholangitis or biliary obstruction. Prophylactic antibiotics have no benefit unless infected necrosis is confirmed. Necrotizing pancreatitis (K85.x2/x3) requires CT at 72 hours and ICU admission. Related condition: COND-024. Guideline: GUIDE-016.

clinical_notes: Specify territory: I63.0x (vertebral artery), I63.1x (basilar artery), I63.2x (carotid artery), I63.3x (cerebral artery anterior), I63.4x (middle cerebral), I63.5x (posterior cerebral). Use Z86.73 for personal history of TIA. Add code for AF (I48.x) if cardioembolic. Door-to-CT time, NIHSS score, and last-known-well time must be documented for quality metrics.
content: ICD-10 code I63.9 designates cerebral infarction, unspecified, representing the most common type of stroke (~87% of all strokes), caused by acute occlusion of a cerebral artery with resulting ischemic brain injury. Time is brain — approximately 1.9 million neurons die every minute during untreated stroke, making rapid diagnosis and reperfusion the paramount priority. Patients present with sudden onset focal neurological deficits: facial droop (face asymmetry), unilateral arm or leg weakness, speech difficulty (aphasia — inability to speak or understand; or dysarthria — slurred speech), sudden vision changes, ataxia, and acute severe headache. NIHSS score quantifies deficit severity and guides treatment decisions. Diagnosis requires emergent non-contrast CT head (rules out hemorrhagic stroke), CT angiography (identifies large vessel occlusion), and MRI diffusion-weighted imaging for early ischemic changes. Blood glucose (LAB-010) is checked immediately — hypoglycemia mimics stroke. Coagulation status (LAB-015) determines alteplase eligibility. Troponin (LAB-012) evaluates for concurrent cardiac event. Per AHA/ASA 2023 guidelines, IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90mg) is the first-line reperfusion therapy when administered within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients. Mechanical thrombectomy is indicated for large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1 MCA, basilar artery) within 24 hours in patients with favorable imaging (ASPECTS ≥6). Blood pressure management requires permissive hypertension: do not treat BP unless above 220/120 (or above 185/110 if alteplase candidate). Aspirin 325mg starts 24-48 hours post-stroke (not within 24 hours of alteplase). Door-to-CT target: 25 minutes; door-to-needle target: 60 minutes. Related condition: COND-029. Guideline: GUIDE-010.

clinical_notes: Specify organism: G00.0 (H. influenzae), G00.1 (pneumococcal), G00.2 (streptococcal), G00.3 (staphylococcal), G00.8 (other). G00.9 when organism pending or not identified. Viral meningitis: G02, G03.x. TB meningitis: A17.0. Cryptococcal: B45.1. CT head BEFORE LP only if papilledema, focal deficits, or altered consciousness — antibiotics must NOT be delayed for CT.
content: ICD-10 code G00.9 designates bacterial meningitis with unspecified organism, representing purulent inflammation of the meninges caused by bacterial pathogens, most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis in adults. Bacterial meningitis carries mortality of 20-30% and significant neurological sequelae in survivors if not treated rapidly. The classic clinical triad of severe headache, fever, and neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity) is present in only 44% of cases — any two of these three symptoms warrant immediate evaluation. Additional features include photophobia, phonophobia, altered mental status, nausea, vomiting, positive Kernig sign (inability to extend knee when hip is at 90 degrees), positive Brudzinski sign (involuntary hip flexion when neck is passively flexed), and in meningococcal meningitis a characteristic petechial or purpuric non-blanching rash indicating meningococcemia requiring immediate isolation and treatment. Critically elevated WBC count with neutrophilic predominance (LAB-004), markedly elevated procalcitonin (LAB-020) and CRP (LAB-023) support bacterial etiology. CSF analysis shows WBC above 1000/uL (neutrophilic predominance), protein above 200 mg/dL, glucose below 40 mg/dL (CSF:serum glucose ratio below 0.4), and positive Gram stain in 60-90%. Per IDSA 2022 guidelines, empiric antibiotics must be administered IMMEDIATELY — within 30 minutes of presentation — without waiting for LP or imaging. Empiric regimen: ceftriaxone 2g IV every 12 hours plus vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg every 8-12 hours; add ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours if age above 50 or immunocompromised for Listeria coverage. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days BEFORE or WITH first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis. Related condition: COND-032. Guideline: GUIDE-012. Disposition: ICU.

clinical_notes: Specify site: M10.01–M10.07 (first MTP joint most common). Tophaceous gout: M1A.x codes (chronic). Drug-induced gout: M10.3x. Gout due to renal impairment: M10.3x. Acute attack typically NOT confirmed by high uric acid alone — serum uric acid may be normal during acute flare. Gold standard is joint aspiration showing negatively birefringent MSU crystals. Must exclude septic arthritis before treating empirically.
content: ICD-10 code M10.9 designates gout, unspecified, representing a crystal arthropathy caused by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and periarticular tissues due to chronic hyperuricemia (serum uric acid above 6.8 mg/dL, LAB-022). Gout most classically affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) but can involve the ankle, knee, wrist, and elbow. Acute gouty arthritis is characterized by dramatic onset of severe joint pain often awakening the patient from sleep, with the affected joint becoming markedly swollen, erythematous, warm, and exquisitely tender — light bedsheet contact causes intense pain. The gold standard diagnosis is joint aspiration revealing negatively birefringent needle-shaped MSU crystals under polarized light microscopy. Serum uric acid (LAB-022) may paradoxically be normal during an acute flare and should never be used to exclude gout; however, hyperuricemia confirms risk. CRP and ESR (LAB-023) are markedly elevated during acute attacks. Serum creatinine (LAB-008) is essential for drug selection, as NSAIDs require adequate renal function, colchicine requires dose adjustment in CKD, and allopurinol dose requires renal adjustment. Septic arthritis must always be excluded in acute monoarthritis as both conditions can coexist. First-line acute treatment includes NSAIDs (indomethacin 50mg TID or naproxen 500mg BID), colchicine (1.2mg then 0.6mg one hour later, most effective within 36 hours), or oral corticosteroids (prednisone 30-40mg for 5 days) if NSAIDs contraindicated. Urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol is indicated after 2 or more attacks per year, targeting serum uric acid below 6 mg/dL. Never initiate or change urate-lowering therapy during an acute attack — it can precipitate or prolong the flare. Febuxostat is an alternative XO inhibitor for allopurinol intolerance.

clinical_notes: T78.2XXA for initial encounter; T78.2XXD for subsequent; T78.2XXS for sequela. Add cause code for specific allergen: T36–T50 for drug-induced, W57.x for insect sting, Z91.0x for food allergy documentation. Always assign the cause of anaphylaxis as an additional code. Epinephrine must be documented as administered or explicitly declined. Minimum 4-6 hour observation is mandatory before discharge.
content: ICD-10 code T78.2XXA designates anaphylactic shock, unspecified, initial encounter — a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction involving multiple organ systems, primarily mediated by IgE-dependent mast cell and basophil degranulation with massive release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins. Common triggers include foods (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish), medications (beta-lactam antibiotics, NSAIDs, contrast media), insect stings (Hymenoptera: bees, wasps, hornets), latex, and exercise. Diagnosis requires rapid onset (typically within minutes to 2 hours) of involvement of two or more organ systems after allergen exposure: skin/mucosal (urticaria, angioedema, flushing), respiratory (stridor from laryngeal edema, bronchospasm, wheezing), cardiovascular (hypotension, tachycardia, syncope), and gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea). A sense of impending doom is a characteristic premonitory symptom. The FIRST and MOST CRITICAL treatment is intramuscular epinephrine 0.3-0.5mg (1:1000 solution) injected into the anterolateral thigh — there is NO absolute contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, and delay in administration is the primary preventable cause of anaphylaxis deaths. Repeat epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if no improvement — there is no maximum dose in life-threatening anaphylaxis. IV normal saline 1-2 liter bolus for hypotension, supplemental oxygen for hypoxia, nebulized albuterol for bronchospasm, diphenhydramine 50mg IV and methylprednisolone 125mg IV are adjuncts — NOT substitutes for epinephrine. Biphasic anaphylaxis occurs in 5-20% of cases, mandating minimum 4-6 hour observation after complete resolution. Discharge with 2 epinephrine auto-injectors and written action plan. Beta-blocker use requires glucagon 1mg IV for refractory hypotension. Related condition: COND-040. Guideline: GUIDE-020.

clinical_notes: Always obtain 12-lead ECG immediately when K+ >5.5 mEq/L — ECG changes drive immediate treatment escalation. Pseudohyperkalemia (hemolyzed specimen): repeat immediately. Code the underlying cause: N18.x (CKD/ESRD), Z79.899 (ACE inhibitor/ARB use), E27.1 (primary hyperaldosteronism). Critical high (K+ >6.0): IV calcium gluconate first, then redistribution, then elimination therapy.
content: ICD-10 code E87.5 designates hyperkalemia, defined as serum potassium above 5.0 mEq/L (LAB-007), a potentially life-threatening electrolyte emergency most dangerous for its cardiac effects. Hyperkalemia is frequently asymptomatic until levels become dangerous, making laboratory detection critical. When symptomatic, patients experience muscle weakness progressing to ascending paralysis, paresthesias, palpitations, nausea, and fatigue. The ECG is the most critical immediate assessment tool: peaked T waves (earliest sign at K+ 5.5-6.5 mEq/L), prolonged PR interval, loss of P waves (K+ 6.5-7.5), widening of QRS complex to sine wave pattern (K+ above 7.5-8.0), and ultimately ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. Always exclude pseudohyperkalemia from hemolyzed blood specimen by repeating the test with a fresh non-hemolyzed sample. Common causes include CKD/ESRD (most common), medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim), adrenal insufficiency, metabolic acidosis (shifts K+ extracellularly), rhabdomyolysis, and tumor lysis syndrome. Renal function (LAB-008) must be assessed to guide management intensity. Treatment is stratified by ECG findings and K+ level: If ECG changes present, IV calcium gluconate 10% 10mL over 2-3 minutes immediately (membrane stabilization — does NOT lower K+); shift K+ intracellularly with regular insulin 10 units IV plus D50 25g, nebulized albuterol 10-20mg, and sodium bicarbonate if metabolic acidosis; remove K+ from body using sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate), patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, furosemide if renal function permits, or emergent hemodialysis for refractory hyperkalemia or severe CKD/ESRD. Discontinue all offending medications. Always treat the underlying cause. Related condition: COND-041.

description: Enterocolitis due to Clostridium difficile, not specified as recurrent
clinical_notes: A04.71 = recurrent CDI; A04.72 = not recurrent. Fulminant CDI adds K59.31 (toxic megacolon) if applicable. Always document: WBC and creatinine for severity classification (non-severe vs severe vs fulminant), causative antibiotic if identifiable, and contact precautions (gown and gloves). Do NOT test for cure — PCR may remain positive for weeks after clinical resolution.
content: ICD-10 code A04.72 designates Clostridioides difficile enterocolitis not specified as recurrent, representing the most common healthcare-associated infectious diarrhea caused by toxigenic Clostridioides difficile (formerly Clostridium difficile) producing toxins A and B that damage colonic epithelium. CDI typically follows disruption of normal gut flora by antibiotics, most commonly fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, and broad-spectrum cephalosporins. Patients present with 3 or more watery unformed stools per 24 hours, abdominal cramping, fever, nausea, and characteristically marked leukocytosis on WBC count (LAB-004), often above 15,000 and sometimes above 30,000 in fulminant disease. Serum creatinine (LAB-008) elevations indicate severe or fulminant disease. Diagnosis requires positive C. diff toxin PCR or toxin enzyme immunoassay. Severity classification drives treatment: non-severe CDI (WBC below 15,000 AND creatinine below 1.5) receives fidaxomicin 200mg BID for 10 days (preferred over vancomycin per IDSA/SHEA 2021 due to lower recurrence rate at similar cost) or oral vancomycin 125mg QID for 10 days; severe CDI (WBC above 15,000 OR creatinine above 1.5) receives oral vancomycin 125mg QID for 10 days; fulminant CDI (hypotension, ileus, or toxic megacolon) receives oral vancomycin 500mg QID plus IV metronidazole 500mg TID with vancomycin enemas added if ileus prevents oral delivery and systemic absorption is needed. Discontinue the inciting antibiotic as soon as clinically feasible. Anti-motility agents (loperamide) are absolutely contraindicated — they worsen toxic megacolon risk. Do NOT retest for cure after clinical resolution (PCR remains positive for weeks). Fecal microbiota transplant achieves 90% cure for second or subsequent recurrences. Related condition: COND-044. Guideline: GUIDE-017.

clinical_notes: Specify cause: E11.641 (T2DM with hypoglycemia without coma), E10.641 (T1DM), E16.0 (drug-induced non-insulin). E16.2 used when cause is not specified. Whipple triad must be documented: symptoms + low glucose + resolution with treatment. Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia requires 24-72 hour monitoring for recurrence. Add underlying DM code when applicable.
content: ICD-10 code E16.2 designates hypoglycemia, unspecified, defined as blood glucose below 70 mg/dL (LAB-010) with clinical significance increasing as glucose drops below 54 mg/dL. Hypoglycemia is most commonly iatrogenic in patients with diabetes on insulin or sulfonylurea therapy, though non-diabetic hypoglycemia from insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency, liver failure, alcohol ingestion, or surreptitious insulin use must be considered. Clinical presentation follows a biphasic pattern: autonomic (adrenergic) symptoms at glucose 60-70 mg/dL include tremor, diaphoresis, palpitations, anxiety, pallor, and hunger; neuroglycopenic symptoms at lower glucose levels include confusion, difficulty concentrating, slurred speech, visual changes, behavioral changes, seizures, and ultimately coma. Diagnosis requires the Whipple triad: symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia, documented low blood glucose at the time of symptoms, and resolution of symptoms when glucose is corrected. For conscious patients who can swallow, the 15-15 rule applies: give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrates (glucose tablets, 4 ounces of juice, or 6 ounces of regular soda), recheck glucose in 15 minutes, repeat if still below 70 mg/dL. For patients unable to swallow or with altered consciousness: IV dextrose 50% (D50W) 25 grams IV push is first choice in hospital setting, or intramuscular/subcutaneous glucagon 1mg (nasal glucagon 3mg is an alternative). Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is uniquely dangerous — these drugs have long half-lives (glipizide 12-24 hours, glyburide 16-24 hours) and can cause recurrent hypoglycemia for 24-72 hours requiring continuous D10W infusion and hospital admission. In non-diabetic unexplained hypoglycemia, check insulin level, C-peptide (elevated with endogenous insulin, low with exogenous), and sulfonylurea screen to evaluate for insulinoma. Related condition: COND-045.

clinical_notes: E27.2 = Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency). Chronic primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease): E27.1. Secondary adrenal insufficiency (pituitary, steroid withdrawal): E27.49. Hydrocortisone must be given BEFORE diagnostic confirmation in suspected crisis. Give thiamine before glucose if concurrent alcoholism. Always add the precipitant code: infection, trauma, surgery. Sick-day rule education essential at discharge.
content: ICD-10 code E27.2 designates Addisonian crisis, representing the life-threatening acute decompensation of adrenal insufficiency with cardiovascular collapse from absolute or relative cortisol deficiency. Adrenal crisis is triggered by physiological stress (infection, surgery, trauma, vomiting/diarrhea causing medication loss) in patients with undiagnosed or undertreated adrenal insufficiency, or by abrupt discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoid therapy. Clinically, adrenal crisis presents as circulatory shock (severe hypotension refractory to IV fluids and vasopressors), altered consciousness, nausea, vomiting, severe abdominal pain mimicking acute abdomen, fever, and hypoglycemia. In primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease, E27.1), chronic features include bronze hyperpigmentation of skin creases, gums, and scars (from elevated ACTH stimulating melanocytes — absent in secondary AI), salt craving, orthostatic hypotension, and distinctive laboratory findings of hyponatremia (LAB-006) with hyperkalemia (LAB-007) from concurrent mineralocorticoid deficiency. Secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease or steroid withdrawal (E27.49) shows hyponatremia without hyperkalemia (mineralocorticoid preserved) and no hyperpigmentation. Hypoglycemia (LAB-010) occurs from cortisol deficiency impairing gluconeogenesis. Morning cortisol below 3 ug/dL is diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency; below 15 ug/dL warrants cosyntropin stimulation testing. Treatment of crisis is an emergency: IV hydrocortisone 100mg bolus IMMEDIATELY — do not wait for diagnostic confirmation when clinical suspicion is high. Follow with 50mg IV every 6-8 hours, aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation (often 2-3 liters in the first hours), and IV dextrose for hypoglycemia. Maintenance: hydrocortisone 15-25mg/day plus fludrocortisone 0.05-0.1mg daily (primary AI only). All patients require sick-day rules education and medical alert bracelet. Related condition: COND-046.

clinical_notes: K92.0 = hematemesis (vomiting blood — upper GI source); K92.1 = melena; K92.2 = GI hemorrhage unspecified. Pair with the underlying cause: K25.x–K28.x for peptic ulcer, I85.x for esophageal varices, K22.3 for Mallory-Weiss tear. Glasgow-Blatchford Score must be documented. Add Z87.21 for personal history of GI hemorrhage. Endoscopy findings should drive ongoing code refinement.
content: ICD-10 code K92.0 designates hematemesis (vomiting of blood), the presenting sign of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, most commonly from peptic ulcers (gastric or duodenal), esophageal or gastric varices in cirrhotic patients, Mallory-Weiss tears, and erosive gastritis or esophagitis. This code should always be paired with the underlying etiology code when identified. Hematemesis may appear as bright red blood (active rapid bleeding) or coffee-ground material (slower bleeding with blood oxidized by gastric acid). Concurrent melena (black tarry stools from digested blood) is common; hematochezia (bright red blood per rectum) suggests massive upper GI bleeding with rapid intestinal transit. Initial hemoglobin (LAB-001) may be normal despite significant hemorrhage due to hemodilution lag — trend is more informative than single values. BUN (LAB-009) elevation disproportionate to creatinine (BUN:Cr ratio above 20:1) indicates upper GI source from protein absorption. Coagulation status (LAB-015) and serum lactate (LAB-019) assess severity and tissue perfusion. The Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) stratifies risk: score 0 allows outpatient management; scores of 1 or above require hospital admission; scores above 6 indicate high risk requiring urgent endoscopy. Per ACG/BSG 2021 guidelines, immediate management includes 2 large-bore peripheral IVs, IV fluid resuscitation, type and crossmatch, pRBC transfusion for hemoglobin below 7 g/dL (or below 9 with massive bleeding or cardiac disease), IV pantoprazole 80mg bolus then 8mg/hr for suspected peptic ulcer, and octreotide 50mcg IV bolus then 50mcg/hr plus IV ceftriaxone 1g daily if variceal bleeding is suspected. EGD within 24 hours for high-risk presentations (within 12 hours if hemodynamically unstable or ongoing active bleeding). Aspirin should be resumed at 3-5 days after hemostasis if cardioprotective indication exists. Related condition: COND-047. Guideline: GUIDE-019.

clinical_notes: F10.239 = alcohol dependence with withdrawal, unspecified. F10.231 = with delirium (delirium tremens). F10.232 = with perceptual disturbances. F10.10 = alcohol abuse without dependence. CIWA-Ar score must be documented. Thiamine MUST precede glucose (Wernicke encephalopathy risk). Withdrawal seizures treated with benzodiazepines — NOT phenytoin.
content: ICD-10 code F10.239 designates alcohol dependence with withdrawal, unspecified, representing the spectrum of central nervous system hyperexcitability that occurs following cessation or reduction of heavy chronic alcohol use. Chronic alcohol exposure causes GABA receptor downregulation (inhibitory system) and NMDA glutamate receptor upregulation (excitatory system), creating a compensatory hyperexcitable state that becomes unmasked when alcohol is withdrawn. Symptoms follow a predictable timeline: minor withdrawal with tremulousness, anxiety, insomnia, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, and nausea begins 6-24 hours after last drink; alcoholic hallucinations (vivid visual, tactile, or auditory hallucinations with preserved orientation) at 12-48 hours; generalized tonic-clonic withdrawal seizures at 12-48 hours (multiple seizures are common — phenytoin is INEFFECTIVE for alcohol withdrawal seizures, benzodiazepines are required); and delirium tremens (F10.231) — the most severe manifestation — at 48-96 hours with confusion, agitation, diaphoresis, fever, and hemodynamic instability carrying 5-15% mortality if untreated. The CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) scale drives treatment: scores above 8 indicate pharmacotherapy requirement; scores above 20 indicate severe withdrawal. Serum potassium (LAB-007) and magnesium (LAB-025) are commonly depleted from vomiting, diarrhea, and poor nutrition — always replete. Liver enzymes (LAB-017) assess hepatic injury severity. First-line treatment is symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide 25-50mg hourly per CIWA or diazepam 10-20mg; lorazepam preferred for hepatic disease due to no active metabolites). Critically: administer IV thiamine 500mg for 3 consecutive days BEFORE any glucose-containing fluids to prevent precipitation of Wernicke encephalopathy (triad of confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) in nutritionally depleted patients. Folate 1mg daily, multivitamin, IV magnesium sulfate 2g, and IV fluids complete supportive care. Related condition: COND-050.

clinical_notes: D65 always requires coding the underlying trigger first: A41.9 (sepsis), O45.x (placental abruption), C92.00 (APL), T79.x (trauma). ISTH DIC score ≥5 = overt DIC. Fibrinogen below 100 mg/dL requires cryoprecipitate. Never treat DIC with heparin unless chronic DIC with thrombosis predominance. TTP (M31.19) must be distinguished from DIC — TTP requires plasma exchange, not blood products.
content: ICD-10 code D65 designates disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a critical syndrome of simultaneous systemic activation of coagulation causing widespread microvascular thrombosis, concurrent consumption of clotting factors and platelets, and secondary fibrinolysis resulting in the paradox of thrombosis and bleeding occurring simultaneously. DIC is never a primary diagnosis — it is always secondary to an underlying trigger, which must be sequenced first. Common triggers include sepsis (most frequent cause, coded A41.9), major trauma with massive tissue injury, obstetric complications (placental abruption O45.x, amniotic fluid embolism O88.x, HELLP syndrome O14.2x), malignancy especially acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, coded C92.00), transfusion reactions, and snake envenomation. Patients present with diffuse bleeding from IV sites, surgical wounds, and mucosal surfaces; petechiae, purpura, and large ecchymoses; digital ischemia or gangrene from microvascular thrombosis; acute multi-organ dysfunction (renal failure, ARDS, hepatic dysfunction); and altered mental status. The ISTH DIC score confirms diagnosis: platelet count below 100,000 (LAB-005), elevated D-dimer or fibrin degradation products (LAB-014), prolonged PT and aPTT (LAB-015), low fibrinogen below 200 mg/dL, and low hemoglobin (LAB-001) from microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on peripheral smear. ISTH score of 5 or above = overt DIC. The most important treatment principle is treating the underlying cause — DIC will not resolve until the trigger is controlled. Supportive transfusion: platelets if below 20,000 or actively bleeding, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen below 100 mg/dL, FFP for prolonged PT/aPTT with active bleeding, pRBCs for symptomatic anemia. Heparin is considered only for chronic DIC with thrombosis predominance (e.g., solid tumor-associated) or purpura fulminans. Distinguish from TTP (M31.19), which requires plasma exchange — not blood products. Related condition: COND-055.

clinical_notes: Specify CKD stage: N18.1 (G1, eGFR ≥90), N18.2 (G2, 60-89), N18.3 (G3a/b, 30-59), N18.4 (G4, 15-29), N18.5 (G5/ESRD, <15 or dialysis). N18.9 only when stage is not documented. Always co-code the cause: I12.9 (CKD due to hypertension), E11.65 (T2DM with hyperglycemia and CKD). eGFR below 30 requires drug dose adjustment for metformin, DOACs, LMWH, and gabapentin.
content: ICD-10 code N18.9 designates chronic kidney disease (CKD), unspecified, representing a progressive and irreversible decline in kidney function persisting for more than 3 months, classified by KDIGO into G1-G5 stages based on eGFR and albuminuria category. CKD is one of the most common and clinically consequential comorbidities affecting drug dosing, cardiovascular risk, and eligibility for numerous therapies. Serum creatinine (LAB-008) and BUN (LAB-009) rise as eGFR declines; serum potassium (LAB-007) requires close monitoring as hyperkalemia is a frequent and dangerous complication in CKD stages 3-5. Common causes include diabetic nephropathy (E11.65, E11.21), hypertensive nephropathy (I12.9), glomerulonephritis (N00-N08), and polycystic kidney disease (Q61.x). CKD significantly affects drug selection across all specialties: metformin is contraindicated when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m², LMWH (enoxaparin) requires dose adjustment or anti-Xa monitoring below eGFR 30, DOACs require dose adjustment or avoidance in advanced CKD, NSAIDs worsen CKD progression and are contraindicated, and aminoglycosides require level-based dosing. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) now have established indication for CKD progression reduction independently of glycemic control, safe down to eGFR 20 for renoprotective benefit. CKD complications include hypertension, anemia of CKD (treat with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and IV iron), secondary hyperparathyroidism, metabolic acidosis, and eventually uremia requiring dialysis when GFR falls below 10-15 mL/min. Annual monitoring: eGFR, urine albumin-creatinine ratio, potassium, bicarbonate, phosphorus, PTH, hemoglobin. Referenced in GUIDE-007 (T2DM management with renal dosing adjustments) and GUIDE-011 (AKI prevention in CKD patients).

description: Rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid factor, unspecified
clinical_notes: M05.x = seropositive RA (RF or anti-CCP positive); M06.9 = seronegative RA. Specify joint involvement when documented: M05.7x (with rheumatoid factor and involvement of unspecified joint). Active RA joint: M05.x1–x9 by joint site. Document DAS28 score for disease activity. MTX contraindicated in pregnancy. TB screening (IGRA) mandatory before biologic initiation.
content: ICD-10 code M05.9 designates rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with rheumatoid factor, unspecified — a chronic systemic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis characterized by synovitis causing joint destruction, extra-articular manifestations, and significant cardiovascular morbidity. RA affects approximately 1% of the global population with a female predominance. Seropositive RA (M05.x) is characterized by positive rheumatoid factor (RF) and/or anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (anti-CCP), which are highly specific for RA and associated with more severe erosive disease. Patients present with morning stiffness lasting more than 60 minutes, symmetric polyarthritis predominantly affecting the MCP, PIP, and wrist joints (DIP joints are typically spared — a key distinguishing feature from osteoarthritis), constitutional symptoms (fatigue, weight loss, low-grade fever), and extra-articular manifestations including rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, and increased cardiovascular risk. CRP (LAB-023) and ESR are elevated during active disease and tracked for treatment response; WBC count (LAB-004) may show leukocytosis during flares or be suppressed by DMARDs. Per ACR 2021 guidelines, the treat-to-target (T2T) strategy drives management with the target of DAS28 remission or low disease activity, assessed every 1-3 months. Methotrexate (MTX) 15-25mg/week plus folic acid 1mg daily is the preferred initial DMARD. If inadequate response after 3 months, add a biologic: anti-TNF (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), IL-6 inhibitor (tocilizumab), JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib, baricitinib), or CTLA4-Ig (abatacept). TNF inhibitors are contraindicated in active serious infection, untreated TB (IGRA must be performed before initiation), demyelinating disease, and NYHA Class III-IV heart failure. MTX is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Related guideline: GUIDE-013.

description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute lower respiratory infection
clinical_notes: J44.0 = COPD with acute lower respiratory infection (pneumonia or acute bronchitis as precipitant). J44.1 = COPD with acute exacerbation (not necessarily infection). J44.9 = COPD unspecified, no exacerbation. Assign the infection code separately: J18.9 (pneumonia), J20.x (acute bronchitis). GOLD group classification (A, B, E) should be documented. Document smoking status with Z87.891 (personal history of tobacco use) or F17.x (current tobacco use).
content: ICD-10 code J44.0 designates chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with acute lower respiratory infection, used when a bacterial or viral lower respiratory infection (pneumonia or acute bronchitis) precipitates COPD worsening. This code contrasts with J44.1 (COPD with acute exacerbation from non-infectious triggers) and J44.9 (stable COPD without exacerbation). Stable COPD is a progressive obstructive airway disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation, chronic productive cough, dyspnea on exertion, and exercise intolerance. GOLD 2024 guidelines classify severity by post-bronchodilator FEV1 (GOLD I–IV) and patient group by symptom burden and exacerbation history (Group A: low symptoms, low risk; Group B: high symptoms, low risk; Group E: high exacerbation risk). Spirometry with post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 is required for diagnosis. Arterial blood gas (LAB-021) documents hypercapnia in advanced disease. Stable COPD management by GOLD group: Group A patients receive short-acting bronchodilator as needed; Group B patients receive long-acting antimuscarinic agent (tiotropium/umeclidinium) as monotherapy; Group E patients receive dual long-acting bronchodilation (LAMA + LABA). ICS is added only when blood eosinophils are above 300 cells/uL with exacerbation history. Smoking cessation is the single most effective intervention for slowing FEV1 decline. Long-term oxygen therapy (minimum 15 hours/day) is the only pharmacological intervention proven to reduce mortality, indicated when PaO2 is 55 mmHg or below at rest or SpO2 is 88% or below. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise tolerance and quality of life for all symptomatic COPD patients. ICS monotherapy increases pneumonia risk and should be avoided. Related guideline: GUIDE-018 (GOLD 2024).

description: Dissection of unspecified site of aorta
clinical_notes: Specify location: I71.01 (type A — ascending, arch, surgical emergency), I71.02 (type B — descending, medical management unless complicated). Stanford Type A requires emergent cardiac surgery; Type B treated with heart rate and BP control (IV labetalol or esmolol, target HR <60, SBP <120). Avoid fibrinolytics — they worsen dissection. CT angiography of chest/abdomen/pelvis is the gold standard imaging.
content: ICD-10 code I71.00 designates aortic dissection of unspecified site, a life-threatening vascular emergency in which blood penetrates through the intima into the aortic media through an intimal tear, creating a false lumen that propagates proximally or distally. Aortic dissection is classified by the Stanford system: Type A involves the ascending aorta (I71.01) — a surgical emergency with mortality increasing approximately 1-2% per hour without operative repair; Type B involves only the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery (I71.02) — managed medically unless complicated by organ ischemia or continued expansion. Patients present with sudden-onset severe tearing or ripping chest pain radiating to the back (interscapular area) — pain is maximal at onset distinguishing it from MI. Associated features include pulse and blood pressure differentials between arms (greater than 20 mmHg asymmetry), aortic regurgitation murmur (Type A), neurological deficits if carotid arteries are involved, and signs of end-organ ischemia. Troponin (LAB-012) and creatinine (LAB-008) may be elevated from coronary or renal malperfusion. CT angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with IV contrast is the gold standard imaging. Avoid fibrinolytics — they are absolutely contraindicated and worsen outcomes. Immediate pharmacological management targets heart rate and blood pressure simultaneously: IV labetalol or esmolol infusion to reduce HR below 60 bpm and systolic BP to 100-120 mmHg, reducing aortic wall shear stress. Type A dissection requires emergent cardiac surgery (within 24 hours). Complicated Type B (ischemia, rapid expansion, uncontrolled pain) requires endovascular repair (TEVAR). Risk factors include uncontrolled hypertension (most important), Marfan syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, cocaine use, and pregnancy.

clinical_notes: Specify etiology: K70.30 (alcoholic cirrhosis), K74.69 (primary biliary cirrhosis), K74.3 (primary sclerosing cholangitis). K74.60 for unspecified. Document Child-Pugh score and MELD score for severity and transplant evaluation. Add complication codes: K65.2 (SBP), I85.00 (esophageal varices), K72.90 (hepatic failure), G92.01 (hepatic encephalopathy). Spironolactone is first-line for ascites.
content: ICD-10 code K74.60 designates unspecified cirrhosis of the liver, representing irreversible end-stage fibrosis of the liver from chronic hepatocellular injury, resulting in portal hypertension, progressive hepatic synthetic dysfunction, and life-threatening complications. Common etiologies include alcoholic liver disease (K70.30, most common in Western countries), chronic hepatitis B (B18.1) and C (B18.2), nonalcoholic steatohepatitis/NASH, autoimmune hepatitis (K75.4), primary biliary cholangitis (K74.3), and hemochromatosis (E83.11). ALT elevation (LAB-017) in cirrhosis may paradoxically be normal or near-normal as hepatocellular mass diminishes. Coagulation (LAB-015) is impaired with elevated INR from reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors (except factor VIII and von Willebrand factor). Platelet count (LAB-005) is low from hypersplenism and thrombopoietin deficiency. Hyponatremia (LAB-007/LAB-006) from SIADH and ascites is a major prognostic marker. Severity is quantified using Child-Pugh score (bilirubin, albumin, INR, encephalopathy, ascites — classes A/B/C) and MELD score (creatinine, bilirubin, INR) for transplant priority. Cirrhosis complications requiring additional codes: ascites managed with sodium restriction and spironolactone 100mg daily (add furosemide 40mg if needed); spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP, K65.2) treated with ceftriaxone 2g IV daily; esophageal varices (I85.00) with non-selective beta-blocker prophylaxis (propranolol or carvedilol); hepatic encephalopathy (G92.01) with lactulose and rifaximin; hepatorenal syndrome; and hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance with ultrasound every 6 months. Liver transplantation is the only curative option. Related guideline: GUIDE-019 (variceal bleeding management).

description: Syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone
clinical_notes: SIADH diagnosis requires: hyponatremia (Na <135), serum hypo-osmolality (<280 mOsm/kg), inappropriately concentrated urine (>100 mOsm/kg), urine Na >40 mEq/L in euvolemic state, and absence of thyroid/adrenal disease. Always identify the cause: malignancy (especially SCLC), CNS disorders (meningitis, stroke), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, TB), medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide). Hypertonic saline ONLY for severe symptomatic hyponatremia — never correct faster than 8 mEq/L per 24 hours.
content: ICD-10 code E22.2 designates Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion (SIADH), the most common cause of hyponatremia in hospitalized patients, caused by non-osmotic release of ADH (arginine vasopressin) leading to free water retention, dilutional hyponatremia, and inappropriately concentrated urine.
