SIADH causes euvolemic hyponatremia — patients appear clinically euvolemic (normal skin turgor, no edema, no orthostasis) distinguishing it from hypovolemic (dehydration, Addison disease) and hypervolemic (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome) causes. Serum sodium (LAB-006) below 135 mEq/L with serum osmolality below 280 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg (inappropriately concentrated despite low serum osmolality), and urine sodium above 40 mEq/L (kidneys retaining water but wasting sodium) confirm SIADH. Thyroid function (hypothyroidism) and morning cortisol (adrenal insufficiency) must be normal to diagnose SIADH. Common causes include CNS disorders (meningitis G00.9 — see GUIDE-012, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, trauma), pulmonary disorders (pneumonia, tuberculosis, ARDS), malignancy (small cell lung cancer produces ectopic ADH — most important paraneoplastic cause), and medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, haloperidol). Symptoms correlate with severity and rate of development: mild hyponatremia (Na 125-135) causes nausea, headache, and cognitive slowing; moderate (Na 115-125) causes confusion and disorientation; severe (Na below 115 or rapid decline) causes seizures, respiratory arrest, and herniation. Treatment: fluid restriction to 800-1000 mL/day for mild-moderate SIADH; hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) only for severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma). Critical safety rule: correct sodium no faster than 8 mEq/L per 24 hours (10-12 mEq/L maximum) — overly rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis), an irreversible devastating neurological complication.

clinical_notes: K72.00 = acute hepatic failure without coma; K72.01 = with coma (hepatic encephalopathy). K72.10 = chronic hepatic failure. Acute liver failure (ALF) definition: INR >1.5 + any degree of encephalopathy within 26 weeks in absence of cirrhosis. Do NOT correct coagulopathy (INR) unless actively bleeding — needed for King's College Criteria prognostication. Acetaminophen toxicity: add T39.1x5A. MELD score required.
content: ICD-10 code K72.90 designates hepatic failure, unspecified without coma, encompassing both acute liver failure (ALF) and decompensated chronic liver disease as the underlying structure requires clinical distinction. Acute liver failure specifically is defined as coagulopathy (INR above 1.5) with any degree of hepatic encephalopathy occurring within 26 weeks in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis. Common causes of ALF include acetaminophen toxicity (most common in the US, dose-dependent and highly treatable with N-acetylcysteine), viral hepatitis (hepatitis A, B, and E), autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury (DILI), ischemic hepatitis (shock liver from cardiovascular collapse), Wilson disease in young patients, and pregnancy-related conditions (acute fatty liver of pregnancy). ALT (LAB-017) may be dramatically elevated above 1000-10,000 U/L in acetaminophen toxicity or ischemic hepatitis; rising INR from coagulopathy (LAB-015) is a key prognostic marker. Serum lactate (LAB-019) elevation reflects tissue hypoperfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction in severe ALF — lactate above 3.5 mmol/L after N-acetylcysteine infusion is a poor prognostic marker in acetaminophen-induced ALF. Critical: do NOT correct the INR with FFP unless the patient is actively bleeding or undergoing a procedure — the INR is used as a prognostic marker in King's College Criteria and artificially normalizing it obscures disease severity assessment. King's College Criteria guide emergency liver transplant evaluation: for acetaminophen-related ALF, pH below 7.30, or combination of INR above 6.5, creatinine above 3.4, and Grade III-IV encephalopathy. N-acetylcysteine (IV or oral) should be given immediately for acetaminophen toxicity within 24 hours of ingestion and is beneficial in non-acetaminophen ALF as well. ICU admission is mandatory. Early hepatology and transplant surgery consultation is essential.

clinical_notes: Thyroid storm (E05.5) is diagnosed by Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45 (points for temp, CNS effects, GI dysfunction, HR, precipitating event, heart failure). E05.01 = thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter (Graves) with thyrotoxic crisis. Treatment sequence: PTU first (blocks synthesis AND peripheral T4→T3 conversion), then iodine 1 hour later (blocks release), propranolol, hydrocortisone. Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis uses E06.4.
content: ICD-10 code E05.5 designates thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm), the most severe and life-threatening complication of thyrotoxicosis, representing a hypermetabolic emergency with systemic decompensation from extreme thyroid hormone excess. Thyroid storm carries a mortality rate of 10-30% even with aggressive treatment. It is typically precipitated in known or undiagnosed hyperthyroid patients by physiological stress: surgery (especially thyroid surgery), infection, trauma, radioactive iodine treatment, abrupt antithyroid drug discontinuation, acute iodine load (contrast media), and MI or PE. Diagnosis is clinical using the Burch-Wartofsky score (BWS): points are assigned for temperature (above 37.2°C), CNS effects (agitation, delirium, seizure, coma), GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice), heart rate (above 90 bpm), presence of a precipitating event, and heart failure grade — BWS of 45 or above indicates thyroid storm. TSH is critically suppressed (LAB-018) with markedly elevated free T4 and free T3. Treatment requires all four components simultaneously: PTU (propylthiouracil) 500-1000mg loading dose then 200-250mg every 4 hours (preferred over methimazole — additionally blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion); potassium iodide (SSKI 5 drops every 6 hours or Lugol solution) given 1 hour AFTER PTU initiation to block thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect — giving iodine before antithyroid drugs provides substrate for synthesis burst); propranolol 60-80mg every 4-6 hours or IV esmolol/labetalol infusion for tachycardia and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion blockade; hydrocortisone 100mg IV every 8 hours to prevent relative adrenal insufficiency (thyroid storm depletes cortisol reserve) and block peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. ICU admission is mandatory. Monitor for AF, heart failure, and hepatic failure.

clinical_notes: D59.0 = drug-induced AIHA; D59.1 = warm antibody AIHA; D59.2 = cold agglutinin disease; D59.9 unspecified. Distinguish from TTP/HUS (M31.19/M31.10) and DIC (D65). Direct Coombs test (DAT) is diagnostic for AIHA. HbA1c may be falsely low in all hemolytic anemias. Plasmapheresis for TTP (NOT AIHA). Corticosteroids are first-line for warm AIHA.
content: ICD-10 code D59.9 designates autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), unspecified, representing a group of acquired disorders in which autoantibodies directed against red blood cell surface antigens cause premature RBC destruction, resulting in anemia and compensatory reticulocytosis. AIHA is classified by thermal reactivity of the antibody: warm AIHA (D59.1, IgG antibodies most active at 37°C, most common type, treated with corticosteroids) and cold agglutinin disease (D59.2, IgM antibodies active at temperatures below 37°C, associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV, lymphoma, and cryoglobulinemia, treated with cold avoidance and rituximab). Drug-induced hemolytic anemia (D59.0) is caused by penicillins, cephalosporins, methyldopa, and quinidine through drug-antibody-RBC interactions. Laboratory hallmarks of hemolytic anemia include: low hemoglobin (LAB-001) with elevated reticulocyte count (compensatory erythropoiesis), elevated indirect bilirubin and LDH from RBC breakdown, low or absent haptoglobin (binds free hemoglobin released from lysed RBCs), and positive direct antiglobulin test (direct Coombs test, DAT) — the key diagnostic test for AIHA confirming IgG or complement (C3d) coating of red cells. Peripheral blood smear shows spherocytes (loss of membrane flexibility from antibody-mediated partial phagocytosis). Platelet count (LAB-005) must be checked: thrombocytopenia concurrent with AIHA defines Evans syndrome (D69.3+D59.1) requiring aggressive immunosuppression. HbA1c (LAB-011) is unreliable and falsely low in all hemolytic anemias. First-line treatment for warm AIHA: prednisone 1-1.5 mg/kg/day, with response expected within 1-3 weeks; rituximab (anti-CD20) for steroid-refractory cases; splenectomy for second-line. Cold agglutinin disease is managed with cold avoidance, rituximab, and sutimlimab (complement inhibitor). Transfusion is challenging due to crossmatch difficulties — use least incompatible units in clinical emergency.

clinical_notes: I10 is the most frequently assigned primary diagnosis code globally. Use I12.x for hypertension with CKD, I13.x for hypertension with heart failure and CKD. Do not use I10 when hypertension is specifically the cause of CKD or HF — use combination codes. Always rule out secondary hypertension in resistant cases: renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, obstructive sleep apnea, Cushing syndrome.
content: ICD-10 code I10 designates essential (primary) hypertension, the most common cardiovascular diagnosis and one of the most frequently assigned codes in clinical practice worldwide, representing sustained elevation of blood pressure above 130/80 mmHg (ACC/AHA 2017 definition) without identified secondary cause. Essential hypertension accounts for 90-95% of all hypertension — secondary causes (renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, obstructive sleep apnea, Cushing syndrome, coarctation of aorta) must be considered in young patients, resistant hypertension (despite 3 medications including a diuretic at maximum doses), or atypical presentations. Serum creatinine (LAB-008) and urine protein-creatinine ratio assess for hypertensive nephropathy; serum sodium (LAB-006) and potassium detect electrolyte abnormalities from antihypertensive medications and secondary causes. Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for stroke, MI, heart failure, and renal disease. Sustained untreated hypertension causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, vascular stiffening, accelerated atherosclerosis, and end-organ damage to brain, heart, and kidneys. Per JNC 8 and ACC/AHA guidelines, pharmacotherapy is initiated when BP is above 130/80 with high cardiovascular risk or above 140/90 in most patients. First-line agents include thiazide diuretics (chlorthalidone preferred over HCTZ for outcomes), ACE inhibitors or ARBs (especially with diabetes or CKD), or dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine). ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred in CKD and diabetes due to additional renoprotective effects. Combination therapy is often required — most patients achieving blood pressure control require 2 or more medications. Target blood pressure is below 130/80 for most patients, below 140/90 for adults above 65 with high comorbidity burden. Related guideline: GUIDE-014 (hypertensive emergency as the critical extreme of this spectrum).

description: Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery without angina pectoris
clinical_notes: I25.10 = CAD without angina. I25.110 = CAD with unstable angina. I25.118 = CAD with other angina. Distinguish stable CAD (I25.10) from ACS (I21.x unstable). Secondary prevention: dual antiplatelet after stent placement (duration depends on stent type — minimum 1 month for BMS, 6-12 months for DES). Cardiac rehabilitation coding: Z87.39 for personal history of MI. Annual stress testing not required in asymptomatic stable CAD.
content: ICD-10 code I25.10 designates atherosclerotic heart disease (CAD) of native coronary artery without angina pectoris, representing the chronic stable phase of coronary artery disease in which atherosclerotic plaque narrows coronary arteries without causing resting chest pain. CAD is the leading cause of death in developed countries and requires lifelong secondary prevention pharmacotherapy. Atherosclerotic plaques causing less than 70% stenosis may remain asymptomatic (I25.10) but are vulnerable to rupture causing ACS. Coronary artery disease is typically diagnosed following ACS events, positive stress testing with imaging, or coronary angiography. High-sensitivity troponin (LAB-012) may show mild chronic elevation in stable CAD without indicating acute injury. Secondary prevention of CAD requires: high-intensity statin therapy (atorvastatin 40-80mg or rosuvastatin 20-40mg daily) targeting LDL-C below 70 mg/dL (below 55 mg/dL for very high-risk patients with recent ACS), aspirin 81mg daily for antiplatelet effect, ACE inhibitor or ARB for left ventricular dysfunction or diabetes, beta-blocker if prior MI or reduced EF, and cardiac rehabilitation. After PCI with stent placement, dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus P2Y12 inhibitor) duration depends on stent type and clinical context: minimum 1 month for bare-metal stent and 6-12 months for drug-eluting stent, extended to 12-36 months in high ischemic risk. Lifestyle modification: tobacco cessation, Mediterranean diet, regular aerobic exercise (minimum 150 minutes/week moderate intensity), and weight management. Annual influenza vaccination reduces cardiovascular events. Monitoring: LDL-C, blood pressure at every visit, HbA1c annually if diabetes, renal function annually, and periodic assessment for anginal symptoms or functional decline. Related guidelines: GUIDE-001 and GUIDE-002 for ACS events.

clinical_notes: Specify: E78.00 (pure hypercholesterolemia), E78.1 (pure hypertriglyceridemia — triglycerides >1000 require urgent treatment to prevent pancreatitis), E78.2 (mixed hyperlipidemia), E78.5 (unspecified). Familial hypercholesterolemia: E78.01. Statin intensity matters for risk: high-intensity (atorvastatin 40-80mg) for ASCVD or equivalent risk. Document 10-year ASCVD risk calculation (Pooled Cohort Equations) for primary prevention decisions.
content: ICD-10 code E78.5 designates hyperlipidemia, unspecified, encompassing abnormal elevations of blood lipid fractions including LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and/or total cholesterol with or without low HDL cholesterol. Hyperlipidemia is one of the most important modifiable cardiovascular risk factors, and lipid management is central to ASCVD risk reduction across primary and secondary prevention. LDL-C is the primary target: in secondary prevention (established ASCVD: prior MI, stroke, PAD), high-intensity statin therapy targeting LDL-C below 70 mg/dL is standard; for very high-risk patients (two or more ASCVD events or ASCVD plus multiple high-risk conditions), target LDL-C below 55 mg/dL with addition of ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor (alirocumab, evolocumab) if goal not achieved. In primary prevention, the 10-year ASCVD risk using Pooled Cohort Equations guides statin initiation: moderate-intensity statin for 7.5-20% risk, high-intensity for 20% or above. Familial hypercholesterolemia (E78.01) requires more aggressive LDL-C targets and often PCSK9 inhibition. Hypertriglyceridemia (E78.1): triglycerides above 500 mg/dL increase pancreatitis risk requiring urgent treatment with fibrates (fenofibrate) or omega-3 fatty acids (icosapentaenoic acid/EPA at 4g/day for cardiovascular benefit); triglycerides above 1000 mg/dL require emergent triglyceride-lowering therapy (NPO, insulin infusion, plasmapheresis in extreme cases, fibrate initiation). Mixed hyperlipidemia (E78.2) with elevated LDL and triglycerides responds to combination statin plus fibrate (avoid statin plus gemfibrozil due to rhabdomyolysis risk — use fenofibrate instead). Lifestyle: saturated fat restriction, dietary soluble fiber, plant sterols, Mediterranean diet, and weight loss. Referenced in GUIDE-007 (T2DM management requires concurrent lipid management with statin therapy for all T2DM patients age 40-75).

clinical_notes: Document BMI: E66.01 (morbid obesity BMI ≥40), E66.09 (other obesity BMI 30-39), E66.9 (unspecified). Assign additional BMI code Z68.x for specificity and risk adjustment. Obesity complicates virtually all other diagnoses — affects drug dosing (weight-based dosing), anesthesia, surgical risk, DOAC dosing (may require anti-Xa monitoring with apixaban/rivaroxaban at BMI >40), and BNP interpretation (falsely low in obesity).
content: ICD-10 code E66.9 designates obesity, unspecified, representing a chronic metabolic disease characterized by excess adiposity (BMI of 30 kg/m² or above) causing systemic health consequences through metabolic, inflammatory, mechanical, and hormonal mechanisms. Obesity is among the most prevalent chronic conditions globally and a major driver of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, sleep apnea, osteoarthritis, fatty liver disease, and certain cancers. More specific coding is preferred when BMI is documented: morbid obesity (BMI 40 or above, E66.01), obesity class 2 (BMI 35-39.9, E66.09), and obesity class 1 (BMI 30-34.9, E66.09) — additional BMI codes Z68.x provide precise quantification for risk adjustment. Obesity significantly impacts clinical management across all specialties: drug dosing is often weight-based (heparin, vancomycin, enoxaparin, gentamicin) requiring dose capping or drug monitoring to avoid toxicity; BNP (LAB-013) is spuriously low in obesity due to increased BNP clearance, reducing its diagnostic utility for heart failure; DOAC effectiveness (apixaban, rivaroxaban) may be reduced at BMI above 40 per ISTH guidance, with anti-Xa monitoring or switching to warfarin considered; endotracheal intubation and regional anesthesia are technically more complex; and bariatric surgery alters drug absorption (particularly extended-release formulations and medications relying on gastric dissolution). Per ADA 2024 guidelines (GUIDE-007), GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide 2.4mg weekly) are first-choice pharmacotherapy for obesity management with T2DM given dual metabolic benefit. Bariatric surgery (metabolic surgery) achieves sustained weight loss and T2DM remission in appropriate candidates with BMI above 35. Comorbidities commonly co-coded with E66.9 include hypertension (I10), type 2 diabetes (E11.9), obstructive sleep apnea (G47.33), hyperlipidemia (E78.5), and GERD (K21.0).

clinical_notes: ARDS requires all Berlin criteria: acute onset within 1 week of clinical insult, bilateral opacities on CXR/CT not explained by effusions or collapse, PaO2/FiO2 (P/F ratio) <300 on PEEP ≥5 cmH2O. Severity: mild P/F 200-300, moderate P/F 100-200, severe P/F <100. Low tidal volume ventilation 6 mL/kg IBW mandatory. Prone positioning for P/F <150 (12-16 hours/day). Avoid excess IV fluids after resuscitation phase.
content: ICD-10 code J80 designates acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a severe diffuse inflammatory lung injury causing non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, hypoxemic respiratory failure, and bilateral alveolar infiltrates, meeting the Berlin 2012 criteria: acute onset within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms, bilateral opacities on chest imaging not fully explained by effusions, lobar or lung collapse, or nodules, absence of respiratory failure fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload (excluded by echocardiography if necessary), and hypoxemia defined by PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 300 mmHg on PEEP or CPAP of 5 cmH2O or above (mild: P/F 200-300; moderate: P/F 100-200; severe: P/F below 100). Common precipitants include sepsis (most common cause, coded A41.9 or R65.20 — see GUIDE-005), pneumonia, aspiration, pancreatitis, major trauma, massive transfusion, and burns. Arterial blood gas (LAB-021) documents severity of hypoxemia and acid-base status; serum lactate (LAB-019) reflects systemic perfusion status. Pathophysiology involves diffuse alveolar damage, alveolar flooding with protein-rich edema fluid, and loss of surfactant causing alveolar collapse and consolidation. The cornerstone of ARDS management is lung-protective mechanical ventilation: tidal volumes of 6 mL/kg ideal body weight (IBW) to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury from overdistension (volutrauma), plateau airway pressure below 30 cmH2O, and sufficient PEEP to prevent cyclic atelectrauma. Prone positioning for at least 12-16 hours per day is indicated for severe ARDS (P/F below 150) — reduces mortality by 16% (PROSEVA trial). Neuromuscular blockade (cisatracurium) may benefit moderate-severe ARDS by improving ventilator synchrony. Conservative fluid management after initial resuscitation reduces ventilator days. Corticosteroids (methylprednisolone) benefit early-moderate ARDS and late fiboproliferative ARDS. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is considered for refractory severe ARDS not responding to conventional management.

clinical_notes: A41.9 = sepsis unspecified organism. A41.01 = MSSA sepsis; A41.02 = MRSA sepsis; A41.51 = gram-negative sepsis; A41.2 = Staph aureus. A41.9 is used when blood cultures are negative or organisms not yet identified. Pair with R65.20 (severe sepsis) or R65.21 (septic shock). Code the source organ first (J18.9 for pneumonia sepsis, N39.0 for urosepsis). Update organism code once cultures finalize.
content: ICD-10 code A41.9 designates sepsis with unspecified organism, used when sepsis is clinically diagnosed but the causative organism has not yet been identified (e.g., blood cultures negative or pending) or when the source of bacteremia cannot be determined. This code represents a different conceptual level than R65.20/R65.21 (severe sepsis/septic shock): A41.9 identifies the infectious etiology while R65.20/21 identifies the systemic response severity. Per ICD-10-CM coding guidelines, the source infection code should be sequenced first, followed by the sepsis code (A41.9) and then severity codes (R65.20/21). Serum lactate (LAB-019) above 2 mmol/L confirms hypoperfusion and mandates the Hour-1 Bundle regardless of blood pressure; lactate above 4 mmol/L meets septic shock criteria even without hypotension (R65.21). Procalcitonin (LAB-020) above 0.5 ng/mL supports bacterial etiology and guides antibiotic escalation; procalcitonin-guided antibiotic discontinuation at 48-72 hours reduces antibiotic duration without increasing mortality. WBC count with differential (LAB-004) shows leukocytosis with left shift (bands) in bacterial sepsis or leukopenia in overwhelming infection. Common source organisms: gram-positive cocci (Staphylococcus aureus — code A41.01 for MSSA, A41.02 for MRSA; Streptococcus pneumoniae — A40.3), gram-negative rods (E. coli — A41.51, Klebsiella — A41.51, Pseudomonas — A41.52), and Candida species (B37.7 for candida sepsis) in immunocompromised hosts. Update to organism-specific code once culture results are finalized — this changes empiric to targeted antibiotic therapy and allows appropriate de-escalation per antibiotic stewardship principles. Related condition: COND-017. Guideline: GUIDE-005 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

clinical_notes: I48.4 = typical (isthmus-dependent) atrial flutter. I48.3 = typical AFL with anticoagulation flag. I48.19 = atypical flutter. On ECG: regular sawtooth flutter waves at 300 bpm with characteristic 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 AV block giving ventricular rate of 150, 100, or 75 bpm. Anticoagulation strategy mirrors AF — apply CHA2DS2-VASc score. Catheter ablation (cavotricuspid isthmus ablation) is curative for typical flutter (>95% success rate).
content: ICD-10 code I48.4 designates typical (cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent) atrial flutter, a regular supraventricular macroreentrant tachycardia circulating counterclockwise around the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium. Atrial flutter generates atrial rates of approximately 300 bpm with characteristic regular sawtooth (negative flutter waves in leads II, III, aVF) or positive flutter waves in V1. Atrioventricular conduction occurs in fixed ratios: 2:1 block gives a ventricular rate of approximately 150 bpm (most common presentation — importantly, any patient presenting with regular tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm requires urgent 12-lead ECG assessment for flutter with 2:1 block), 3:1 block gives approximately 100 bpm, and 4:1 block gives approximately 75 bpm. TSH (LAB-018) must be checked to exclude thyrotoxicosis as a precipitant, and BNP (LAB-013) may be elevated from tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy. Atrial flutter carries the same thromboembolic risk as atrial fibrillation — anticoagulation decisions follow identical CHA2DS2-VASc criteria per ACC/AHA/HRS 2023 guidelines (GUIDE-004). Rate control with beta-blockers or diltiazem is more challenging in flutter than in AF. Electrical cardioversion is highly effective (often low-energy 50-100J) and is preferred for hemodynamically unstable patients. Chemical cardioversion with ibutilide 1mg IV is an option. Catheter ablation targeting the cavotricuspid isthmus is the definitive curative treatment with greater than 95% success rate and low recurrence, strongly preferred over long-term antiarrhythmic drug therapy. Patients with flutter managed with flecainide or propafenone must also receive an AV nodal blocking agent (beta-blocker or diltiazem) to prevent 1:1 conduction that can be life-threatening. Typical flutter frequently co-exists with AF — ablation of flutter may unmask AF in susceptible patients.

clinical_notes: E10.x = type 1 DM (autoimmune, absolute insulin deficiency). E11.x = type 2 DM. Do not interchange — the distinction affects drug coverage, clinical protocols, and coding compliance. E10.9 applies without complications; add complication codes when documented. Type 1 DM requires continuous insulin; metformin adjunct is sometimes used. Monitor for DKA (E10.10) and hypoglycemia (E10.641). Annual C-peptide may distinguish T1DM from LADA/T2DM when diagnosis is uncertain.
content: ICD-10 code E10.9 designates type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) without complications, representing autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency and complete dependence on exogenous insulin for survival. T1DM accounts for 5-10% of all diabetes cases and typically presents in childhood or young adulthood (peak onset ages 10-14), though latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA) can present at any age. Autoimmune markers include islet cell antibodies (ICA), anti-GAD65 antibodies (most sensitive), anti-IA-2 antibodies, and anti-zinc transporter 8 (anti-ZnT8) antibodies. C-peptide is low or undetectable in T1DM (confirming absolute beta-cell failure), distinguishing it from T2DM where C-peptide is normal or elevated. Blood glucose (LAB-010) and HbA1c (LAB-011) monitoring follow the same targets as T2DM (HbA1c below 7% for most adults, below 7.5% if hypoglycemia-prone). Serum potassium (LAB-007) is critical during DKA management — always confirm potassium above 3.5 mEq/L before starting insulin. Intensive insulin therapy requires a basal-bolus regimen: long-acting insulin (glargine, detemir, degludec) for basal coverage and rapid-acting insulin (lispro, aspart, glulisine) for prandial coverage, with correction doses for hyperglycemia — carbohydrate-to-insulin ratio and insulin sensitivity factor individualized for each patient. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with time-in-range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL as target above 70%) and closed-loop insulin delivery (artificial pancreas) are current standards of care improving glycemic control and reducing hypoglycemia. T1DM patients are at high risk for DKA (E10.10) — any infection, insulin omission, or pump failure can precipitate DKA. Associated autoimmune conditions: Hashimoto thyroiditis (30%), celiac disease (10%), Addison disease (rare but important). Guideline: GUIDE-008 for DKA management protocol.

clinical_notes: I50.31 = acute HFpEF (preserved EF, diastolic HF). I50.21 = acute HFrEF (reduced EF, systolic HF). I50.41 = acute combined systolic and diastolic HF. EF must be documented to assign these specific codes. HFpEF (EF ≥50%) represents >50% of all HF cases. Guideline-directed therapy for HFpEF differs from HFrEF — SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) now have Class IIa recommendation for HFpEF.
content: ICD-10 code I50.31 designates acute diastolic (congestive) heart failure, representing heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in its acute decompensated form. HFpEF is defined as heart failure symptoms with left ventricular ejection fraction of 50% or above on echocardiography, caused by impaired ventricular relaxation and reduced compliance (diastolic dysfunction) rather than reduced systolic contractility. HFpEF now accounts for more than 50% of all heart failure diagnoses and is increasing in prevalence due to aging populations and rising rates of obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation — the four key comorbidities driving HFpEF. BNP or NT-proBNP (LAB-013) elevation confirms the hemodynamic stress of fluid overload even in HFpEF. Creatinine (LAB-008) and potassium (LAB-007) require monitoring during diuretic therapy. Clinically, HFpEF presents identically to HFrEF: dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, lower extremity edema, pulmonary crackles, and elevated filling pressures on echocardiography (elevated E/e' ratio above 14 supports diastolic dysfunction). Acute decompensation is managed similarly to HFrEF: IV diuresis targeting 3-5 liter output per day, oxygen supplementation, sodium and fluid restriction. Per ACC/AHA/HFSA 2022 guidelines (GUIDE-003), SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin 10mg daily, empagliflozin 10mg daily) have Class IIa recommendation for HFpEF, reducing heart failure hospitalizations in clinical trials (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER). ARBs (candesartan) and spironolactone have weaker evidence in HFpEF compared to HFrEF. Beta-blockers do not reduce mortality in HFpEF but are used for rate control in concurrent AF. Cardiac rehabilitation improves functional capacity. Unlike HFrEF, most guideline-directed medical therapies proven for HFrEF have not demonstrated mortality benefit in HFpEF.

description: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
clinical_notes: N30.0 = acute cystitis; N10 = acute pyelonephritis; N39.0 = UTI site not specified. Always code when organism identified: B96.20 (E. coli UTI — most common), B96.5 (Pseudomonas), etc. Urosepsis must be coded as sepsis (A41.9 + R65.x) with urinary source — 'urosepsis' alone is insufficient coding. Asymptomatic bacteriuria (R82.71) should NOT be treated unless pregnancy or pre-urologic procedure.
content: ICD-10 code N39.0 designates urinary tract infection, site not specified — a common bacterial infection of the urinary system most often caused by Escherichia coli (70-80% of community-acquired UTIs), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus saprophyticus (especially young sexually active women), Enterococcus faecalis, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in catheter-associated or hospital-acquired infections. WBC count (LAB-004) may show leukocytosis in complicated UTI or pyelonephritis; creatinine (LAB-008) is elevated in cases progressing to sepsis-related AKI. Uncomplicated lower UTI (cystitis, N30.0) in otherwise healthy non-pregnant premenopausal women presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort, diagnosed by positive urine dipstick (leukocyte esterase and/or nitrites) or urinalysis (>10 WBCs/hpf). Treatment: nitrofurantoin 100mg extended-release BID for 5 days or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (if susceptibility confirmed) for 3 days, or fosfomycin 3g single dose. Fluoroquinolones should be reserved for more complex UTIs due to resistance pressure and adverse effect profile. Complicated UTI (pyelonephritis N10) with fever, flank pain, nausea, and costovertebral angle tenderness requires blood cultures, urine culture, and typically IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone 1-2g IV daily or fluoroquinolone if susceptibility documented). Urosepsis — a UTI progressing to sepsis — requires the full sepsis coding sequence: A41.9 (sepsis with unspecified organism) + N39.0 (source) + R65.20 or R65.21 (severity), NOT merely 'urosepsis.' Asymptomatic bacteriuria (R82.71) should NOT be treated with antibiotics unless in pregnancy (increases risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labor) or prior to urological procedures — overtreatment drives antibiotic resistance. Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) uses T83.511A and is a preventable hospital-acquired condition tracked by CMS.

clinical_notes: Specify location: L03.011 (right finger), L03.111 (right arm), L03.211 (right trunk), L03.311 (right foot). L03.90 when site not documented. Differentiate from necrotizing fasciitis (M72.6 — surgical emergency), DVT (I82.4x), and erysipelas (A46). LRINEC score helps risk-stratify necrotizing soft tissue infection. Mark the erythema border to track progression. Blood cultures are low-yield in non-bacteremic cellulitis — discouraged without systemic signs.
content: ICD-10 code L03.90 designates cellulitis, unspecified site, representing an acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue most commonly caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci (Group A Streptococcus pyogenes) and Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA. Cellulitis presents with localized erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness, and occasionally lymphangitis and regional lymphadenopathy. Systemic signs including fever, chills, and leukocytosis (LAB-004) indicate more severe infection. CRP (LAB-023) and procalcitonin (LAB-020) are elevated in proportion to severity. The critical clinical priority is distinguishing cellulitis from life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis (M72.6 — surgical emergency): necrotizing fasciitis features disproportionate pain, rapid progression, skin discoloration (gray or dusky hue), bullae, crepitus, systemic sepsis, and a LRINEC score above 6 indicating high risk. CT imaging showing gas in fascial planes or magnetic resonance imaging can confirm necrotizing fasciitis when diagnosis is unclear — surgical exploration is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. Differentials also include DVT (compression ultrasound excludes), erysipelas (A46, more superficial well-demarcated infection with Streptococcus, treated identically), and contact dermatitis (bilateral, not unilateral). Mark the erythema borders with a skin marker on presentation to monitor progression or regression. Outpatient treatment for mild non-purulent cellulitis: oral cefalexin 500mg QID or amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5-7 days; add trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for MRSA coverage if purulence or risk factors. Inpatient IV therapy (cefazolin or oxacillin) for systemic signs, rapid progression, failure to improve on oral therapy after 48-72 hours, or immunocompromise. MRSA cellulitis (vancomycin IV or TMP-SMX orally) is more commonly associated with purulent or abscess-forming infections. Blood cultures are low-yield and not routinely recommended unless systemic sepsis is present.

clinical_notes: I27.0 = primary (idiopathic/heritable) PH (Group 1 PAH). I27.20 = secondary PH unspecified (Groups 2-5). WHO Group classification: Group 1 (PAH — idiopathic, heritable, drug-induced), Group 2 (left heart disease), Group 3 (lung disease/hypoxia), Group 4 (CTEPH), Group 5 (multifactorial). Diagnosis requires right heart catheterization: mPAP >20 mmHg + PVR >2 Wood units + PCWP ≤15. Group 1 PAH uses targeted therapies (endothelin antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors, prostanoids).
content: ICD-10 code I27.0 designates primary pulmonary hypertension, now classified as Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) by the WHO classification, characterized by elevated pulmonary arterial pressure from primary vascular disease (vasoproliferation, vasoconstriction, thrombosis) in the absence of other identifiable causes. PAH is diagnosed by right heart catheterization showing mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) above 20 mmHg, pulmonary vascular resistance above 2 Wood units, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg. This distinguishes it from left heart disease-related PH (Group 2, I27.22), the most common cause of elevated pulmonary pressures. Subtypes include idiopathic PAH (I27.0), heritable PAH (BMPR2 gene mutations most common), drug/toxin-induced PAH (anorexigens, methamphetamine, dasatinib), and PAH associated with connective tissue disease (scleroderma most commonly), HIV, portal hypertension, and congenital heart disease. Patients present insidiously with progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, dizziness, syncope on exertion (ominous — indicates critically reduced cardiac output), and eventually right heart failure with peripheral edema. BNP (LAB-013) elevation correlates with RV dysfunction severity and prognosis; troponin (LAB-012) elevation indicates RV ischemia and severe prognosis. WHO functional class (I-IV) guides treatment intensity. Targeted PAH therapies by pathway: endothelin receptor antagonists (ambrisentan, macitentan, bosentan) block ET-1-mediated vasoconstriction; PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) promote vasodilation via nitric oxide/cGMP pathway; prostanoid analogues (epoprostenol IV — gold standard for severe PAH, treprostinil SC/inhaled) are the most potent vasodilators. Combination upfront therapy is now standard for high-risk PAH. Lung transplantation for refractory disease. Avoid pregnancy (extremely high mortality risk in PAH).

clinical_notes: E87.1 is the code for clinical hyponatremia (Na <135 mEq/L). Always determine volume status (hypovolemic, euvolemic, hypervolemic) to identify cause before treating. Euvolemic: SIADH (E22.2), hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency. Hypovolemic: vomiting, diarrhea, diuretics, Addisonian crisis (E27.2). Hypervolemic: heart failure (I50.x), cirrhosis (K74.6x), nephrotic syndrome. Never correct faster than 8 mEq/L/24h — osmotic demyelination syndrome risk.
content: ICD-10 code E87.1 designates hypo-osmolality and hyponatremia, defined as serum sodium below 135 mEq/L (LAB-006), the most common electrolyte disorder in hospitalized patients with significant morbidity and mortality if improperly managed. Hyponatremia is classified by volume status, which is the critical first step in determining etiology and treatment: hypovolemic hyponatremia (from sodium and water losses with relatively more sodium loss — diarrhea, vomiting, diuretics, Addisonian crisis, third-spacing) characterized by dry mucosa, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, and orthostasis; euvolemic hyponatremia (water retention without sodium loss — SIADH E22.2, hypothyroidism E03.9, adrenal insufficiency E27.2, psychogenic polydipsia) without edema or orthostasis; and hypervolemic hyponatremia (sodium and water both retained but relatively more water — dilutional; heart failure I50.x, cirrhosis K74.6x, nephrotic syndrome) with edema, ascites, or pleural effusions. Symptom severity correlates with both the absolute sodium level and the rate of decline: mild hyponatremia (Na 125-135 mEq/L) causes nausea, headache, and cognitive slowing; moderate (Na 115-125) causes confusion and lethargy; severe (Na below 115 or rapid decline) causes seizures, respiratory arrest, cerebral herniation, and death. Treatment principles: for hypovolemic hyponatremia — replace volume with isotonic saline (addresses both volume deficit and sodium); for euvolemic SIADH — fluid restriction to 800-1000 mL/day and treat underlying cause; for hypervolemic hyponatremia — address underlying cause with diuresis. Hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) infusion is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma) — initial bolus of 100-150 mL over 10-15 minutes, repeat up to 3 times if seizures persist. Critical safety rule: correct sodium at a maximum rate of 8 mEq/L per 24 hours (or 1-2 mEq/L per hour acutely during seizures, stopping once seizures resolve) — overly rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis), an irreversible catastrophic neurological complication.

clinical_notes: D51.0 = pernicious anemia (autoimmune, intrinsic factor deficiency); D51.3 = B12 deficiency from dietary insufficiency; D51.9 = unspecified. Always check anti-intrinsic factor antibodies and anti-parietal cell antibodies to distinguish pernicious anemia from other causes. Metformin use causes B12 malabsorption — annual B12 monitoring required after 4+ years. Neurological manifestations (subacute combined degeneration) can occur without severe anemia.
content: ICD-10 code D51.9 designates vitamin B12 deficiency anemia, unspecified, representing a macrocytic megaloblastic anemia resulting from inadequate B12 for DNA synthesis, causing impaired nuclear maturation in rapidly dividing cells including erythroid precursors. Hemoglobin (LAB-001) is reduced and MCV (LAB-002) is elevated above 100 fL (macrocytosis), with hypersegmented neutrophils (5 or more lobes in any neutrophil, or any 6-lobed neutrophil) on peripheral blood smear serving as a pathognomonic finding. Serum B12 below 200 pg/mL is diagnostic; methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine elevations confirm true B12 deficiency even when serum B12 is in the borderline range (200-300 pg/mL). Common causes include pernicious anemia (D51.0 — autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells causing intrinsic factor deficiency; diagnosed by positive anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies), strict vegan diet without supplementation (B12 is found only in animal products), gastric bypass surgery (prevents intrinsic factor secretion), Crohn disease involving the terminal ileum (site of B12-intrinsic factor complex absorption), prolonged metformin use (reduces B12 absorption by calcium-dependent mechanism — annual B12 monitoring is recommended per ADA guidelines after 4 or more years of metformin therapy, GUIDE-007), and fish tapeworm infection (Diphyllobothrium latum). Critically, B12 deficiency causes neuropsychiatric manifestations (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord — paresthesias, loss of proprioception, gait ataxia, and dementia) that can occur without significant anemia and are potentially irreversible if not treated promptly. Treatment: for pernicious anemia and severe deficiency — IM or SC cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily for 7 days, then weekly for 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong; high-dose oral B12 (1000-2000 mcg daily) is equally effective for non-pernicious causes due to passive absorption. Neurological recovery takes weeks to months; complete recovery may not occur if deficiency was prolonged.

clinical_notes: D64.9 is a non-specific code — always attempt to identify specific anemia type: D50.x (iron deficiency), D51.x (B12 deficiency), D52.x (folate deficiency), D55-D58 (hemolytic anemias), D59 (acquired hemolytic), D61 (aplastic). MCV is the first discriminator: microcytic <80 fL, normocytic 80-100 fL, macrocytic >100 fL. Anemia of chronic disease/CKD: D63.x (secondary anemia). Always identify and treat the underlying cause — D64.9 coding alone is insufficient for quality documentation.
content: ICD-10 code D64.9 designates anemia, unspecified — a non-specific code to be used only when a more specific anemia type cannot be identified based on available clinical information. Anemia is defined as hemoglobin below 12 g/dL in women and below 13 g/dL in men (LAB-001) by WHO criteria. The diagnostic workup follows a systematic algorithmic approach based on MCV (LAB-002): microcytic anemia (MCV below 80 fL) suggests iron deficiency (confirmed by low ferritin LAB-003), thalassemia (normal or low ferritin with disproportionately low MCV for degree of anemia — Mentzer index), anemia of chronic disease (low-normal MCV, low ferritin with normal or high ferritin), or lead poisoning; normocytic anemia (MCV 80-100 fL) suggests anemia of chronic disease/inflammation, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, early iron deficiency, or mixed nutritional deficiency; and macrocytic anemia (MCV above 100 fL) suggests B12 deficiency (D51.x), folate deficiency (D52.x), alcohol use disorder, hypothyroidism, liver disease, or medication effects (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, zidovudine). Anemia of chronic disease (D63.x) is the most common anemia in hospitalized patients — caused by inflammatory cytokines (IL-6) stimulating hepcidin, sequestering iron in macrophages and reducing erythropoiesis, characterized by low serum iron, low TIBC, and normal or elevated ferritin distinguishing it from iron deficiency. Reticulocyte count and index distinguish hypoproliferative anemia (low reticulocyte, bone marrow failure or nutritional) from hyperproliferative (high reticulocyte, hemolysis or blood loss). Transfusion thresholds per evidence-based guidelines: hemoglobin below 7 g/dL in most hospitalized patients (TRICC trial), below 8 g/dL in active cardiac ischemia or post-cardiac surgery. Always identify and specifically code the anemia type — D64.9 is a documentation gap for quality measures.

clinical_notes: G47.33 = obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). G47.31 = primary central sleep apnea. G47.37 = central sleep apnea in conditions classified elsewhere (heart failure-related). OSA is a major comorbidity affecting cardiovascular risk, arrhythmia (especially AF), metabolic syndrome, and perioperative risk. Always screen with STOP-BANG questionnaire preoperatively. Untreated OSA in heart failure worsens outcomes — CPAP therapy required. OSA-related hypoxia assessed by nocturnal oximetry or ABG (LAB-021). BNP may be elevated from OSA-associated pulmonary hypertension.
content: ICD-10 code G47.33 designates obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by repetitive episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep, causing oxygen desaturation, sleep fragmentation, and sympathetic nervous system activation with resulting cardiovascular and metabolic consequences. OSA affects an estimated 10-30% of adults, with obesity (E66.9) being the predominant risk factor. Diagnosis requires polysomnography showing an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 5 or more events per hour with symptoms, or AHI of 15 or more regardless of symptoms: mild OSA (AHI 5-15), moderate (AHI 15-30), severe (AHI above 30). STOP-BANG questionnaire (Snoring, Tired, Observed apnea, blood Pressure, BMI above 35, Age above 50, Neck circumference above 40cm, Gender male) is a validated preoperative screening tool — score of 5-8 indicates high risk. Nocturnal hypoxemia documented by oximetry or sleep-study oxygen nadir; in severe OSA, daytime ABG (LAB-021) may show chronic hypercapnia suggesting obesity hypoventilation syndrome. OSA drives multiple comorbidities: systemic hypertension (I10, from nocturnal sympathetic surges), AF (I48.91, from atrial stretch and hypoxia), pulmonary hypertension (I27.0, from chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction with elevated BNP LAB-013), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, metabolic syndrome, impaired insulin resistance, and right heart failure (cor pulmonale) in severe untreated OSA. Perioperative risk: OSA patients are at substantially increased risk for post-extubation respiratory failure and require careful opioid dosing, continuous monitoring, and CPAP availability. First-line treatment is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy, which normalizes AHI, reduces blood pressure, improves daytime sleepiness, and reduces cardiovascular events. Alternatives include mandibular advancement devices for mild-moderate OSA or hypoglossal nerve stimulation for PAP-intolerant patients.
